lessons.briefing:
# V3·C1 — JSONB storage, operators and containment

You have used `products.attributes` since lesson 19 and indexed it in
lesson 42, but always as a black box: arrows go in, values come out. That
works until the day a containment test returns rows you did not expect, or
a document that looked five bytes long turns out to cost two kilobytes, or
`-> 'color' = 'red'` refuses to compile and you cannot say why in one
sentence.

This sector opens the box. Not for trivia, for three practical reasons.
First, containment is the operator your indexes accelerate, and its rules
are subtler than "contains". Second, a document column has three distinct
ways of holding nothing, and code that confuses them silently loses rows.
Third, jsonb is a *value*, not a mutable structure: every write rewrites
the whole document, and knowing that changes how you design writes.

## Concept

`jsonb` is not stored text. On the way in, PostgreSQL parses the document
into a binary tree of headers, offsets and scalars:

```sql
SELECT '{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}'::json  AS as_json,
       '{"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}'::jsonb AS as_jsonb;
-- as_json  : {"b": 1, "a": 2, "a": 3}     <- the exact bytes you typed
-- as_jsonb : {"a": 3, "b": 1}             <- parsed, sorted, deduplicated
```

Three consequences fall straight out of that one line:

- **Key order is not preserved.** Keys sort by length, then bytewise. An
  application that round-trips a document through `jsonb` and compares the
  serialized text against what it sent will see a diff.
- **Duplicate keys collapse**, last one wins. `json` keeps both and hands
  you the last one on lookup; `jsonb` throws the earlier one away at parse
  time.
- **Whitespace is gone**, so two documents that differ only in formatting
  are equal. `jsonb` equality is structural, which is exactly what you want
  and exactly what text comparison cannot give you.

The operator set is bigger than the two arrows you know:

```sql
attributes ->  'color'                 -- jsonb  ("red", with the quotes)
attributes ->> 'color'                 -- text   (red)
attributes #>  '{tags,0}'              -- jsonb, by path
attributes #>> '{tags,0}'              -- text, by path
attributes @>  '{"color": "red"}'      -- containment: left contains right
attributes <@  '{"color": "red"}'      -- contained by
attributes ?   'color'                 -- top-level key exists
attributes ?|  array['color', 'size']  -- any of these keys exists
attributes ?&  array['color', 'size']  -- all of these keys exist
attributes ||  '{"clearance": true}'   -- shallow merge, returns a new value
attributes -   'tags'                  -- delete a top-level key
attributes #-  '{tags,0}'              -- delete at a path
```

Two things about that list are worth memorising now. `@>` and the three
`?` operators are the ones a default GIN index answers, so express
predicates with them where you can. And `||`, `-` and `#-` are *functions
in operator clothing*: they return a new document, they modify nothing.
There is no in-place edit of a jsonb value anywhere in PostgreSQL.

Containment has one rule that catches everyone. It is recursive and it is
happy inside arrays, so `attributes @> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` means "tags
includes eco" — but the nesting on the right must match the nesting on the
left. `'{"tags": ["eco"]}'` is contained in `'{"tags": ["eco","limited"]}'`;
`'{"tags": "eco"}'` is not, because on the left the value is an array and
on the right it is a scalar. The one deliberate exception is at the top
level: a scalar counts as contained in a one-element array, so
`'["eco"]'::jsonb @> '"eco"'::jsonb` is true. That special case exists only
at the top level, and it exists mostly to trip you up.

Finally, the three nothings:

```sql
SELECT attributes ->  'discount'   IS NULL,   -- key missing?  -> true
       attributes ->> 'discount'   IS NULL,   -- text of it    -> true
       jsonb_typeof(attributes -> 'discount') -- NULL, not 'null'
FROM products WHERE id = 1;
```

A missing key yields SQL NULL. A key present with the JSON literal `null`
yields a *non-null* jsonb value whose `jsonb_typeof` is the string
`'null'` and whose `->>` is SQL NULL. So `->>` cannot tell "absent" from
"explicitly null", and `?` can: `attributes ? 'discount'` is the only test
that answers "is the key there at all".

## Exercise 1 — what type is that

Read the type of each value with `jsonb_typeof` for the first ten products.
The point is to see that a document knows its own types, and that a missing
key is not a JSON type at all.

## Exercise 2 — containment, not equality

Count the products matching a two-key document. Written with `@>` it is one
predicate and it is indexable; written as two `->>` comparisons it is two
predicates and it is not.

## Exercise 3 — does the key exist

`?&` over the three attribute keys, which answers "is this document
complete" for ten thousand rows at once, and does it without extracting a
single value.

## Exercise 4 — subtraction

`-` removes a top-level key and `#-` removes an element at a path. Both
return a new document; the table does not change, and the exercise makes
you prove it.

## Exercise 5 — merge is shallow

`||` merges at the top level only. You will add a key with it, then watch
the same operator destroy a nested object rather than merging into it.

## Exercise 6 — contained by

`<@` reverses the direction and answers a question `@>` cannot: which
products draw *both* their tags from a fixed set.

## Exercise 7 — the three nothings

A small hand-built table with a missing key, a JSON null and a SQL NULL in
it. You will classify each row and produce the report that tells the three
apart.

## Exercise 8 — the key inventory

`jsonb_each` turns a document into rows. Use it to build the report every
team eventually needs for a document column nobody wrote down: which keys
exist, and how many distinct values each one carries.

## Challenge — normalise a document

Build a derived document per product: tags removed, a computed price band
added, colour kept. Three operators, one expression, no update.

## Review 1 — the same question two ways

Answer one question with containment and with extract-and-cast in the same
query, and prove the two counts agree. When they do not, one of them is
wrong about types, and it is never the containment version.

# Reading - v3c01_jsonb_storage

Everything in this sector follows from one design decision: `jsonb` parses
on the way in. Sorted keys, structural equality, containment, indexability
and the whole-document rewrite cost are all downstream of that decision.

## Notes

**Parse-on-write is the whole story.** `json` validates and stores bytes;
`jsonb` builds a binary container tree. So `json` inserts faster and reads
slower, preserves formatting, key order and duplicate keys, and supports no
operators worth indexing. Choose `jsonb` unless the exact bytes are the
point — a signed webhook body you must re-verify, an audit copy of a
third-party response.

**Keys are sorted by length, then bytes.** Not alphabetically. `{"z": 1,
"aa": 2}` renders as `{"z": 1, "aa": 2}` because `z` is shorter. Do not
write assertions against the text rendering of a jsonb value; assert on
`jsonb` equality, which is structural and formatting-independent.

**`->` versus `->>` is a type question, not a style question.** `->`
returns `jsonb`, so `-> 'color'` is the two-character-longer string
`"red"`, quotes included. `->>` returns `text`. The compile error people
hit is comparing `jsonb` to a string literal; the *silent* bug is comparing
extracted text numerically, because `'996' < '99'` is true in text order.
Cast: `(payload ->> 'value')::int`.

**Containment is recursive and array-aware.** `@>` asks whether every key
and value of the right document appears somewhere correspondingly in the
left, at any depth, and treats a right-hand array as a subset test against
the left-hand array. It ignores array order and it ignores extra keys. The
only asymmetry is the top-level scalar-in-array case.

**Existence operators look at top-level keys only.** `?`, `?|` and `?&`
test object keys at the top level, or, if the value is an array of strings,
membership in that array. `attributes -> 'tags' ? 'eco'` therefore works
and reads well. Nested object keys need a path first.

**`||` merges shallowly.** Matching keys are replaced wholesale, not merged
recursively. It also concatenates arrays, and merging an object with a
scalar wraps things in ways that are rarely what you meant. When you catch
yourself wanting a deep merge, ask why the nesting exists.

**`-` takes a key, an index, or an array of keys.** `doc - 'tags'` deletes
a key; `doc - 0` deletes an array element; `doc - array['a','b']` deletes
several keys. `#-` takes a path. None of them mutate: they return a value,
which you then have to store somewhere if you want it kept.

**The three nothings.** Missing key: `->` is SQL NULL, `?` is false. JSON
null: `->` is a jsonb value, `jsonb_typeof` is `'null'`, `->>` is SQL NULL,
`?` is true. SQL NULL in the column itself: every operator returns NULL and
your `WHERE` clause quietly drops the row. Decide which of the three your
schema means, and write the test that distinguishes it.

**Equality and ordering exist, and only equality is useful.** Two jsonb
values are equal when their parsed structures match, so whitespace and key
order cannot make them differ. There is also a total order — objects sort
above arrays, which sort above booleans, then numbers, then strings, then
null, with objects compared first by key count — which means `ORDER BY doc`
and `GROUP BY doc` and `DISTINCT doc` all work. Almost nobody wants that
ordering for display; what they want it for is deduplication, and for that
it is exactly right.

**Documents are values, so they compose.** `jsonb` columns can be grouped,
aggregated, passed to functions, returned from CTEs and compared. The
practical upshot is that `count(DISTINCT attributes)` is a legal and
meaningful query, and that a derived document computed in a select list is
as first-class as a derived number. Nothing about a document column is
special-cased in the executor.

**Size is not what the text looks like.** `pg_column_size` on a jsonb value
counts headers, `JEntry` words and numeric overhead. Small documents are
often *larger* than their text rendering; large repetitive ones compress
below it. Measure before you argue about it.

## ex1 — what type is that

Types come out as the strings `object`, `array`, `string`, `number`,
`boolean`, `null`. A key that is absent gives SQL NULL instead — a
different kind of answer, from a different level of the system.

## ex2 — containment, not equality

Two spellings of one question. Run both in the lab under `EXPLAIN` after
lesson 42's GIN index exists and watch only one of them use it.

## ex3 — does the key exist

Note what you did not do: extract a value. Existence is answered from the
key entries alone, which is why GIN with the default operator class can
answer it and `jsonb_path_ops` cannot.

## ex4 — subtraction

The result is a new document in the result set. Query the table again
afterwards and see the original untouched; that is the whole lesson.

## ex5 — merge is shallow

The second half of this exercise is the useful half. Watch the nested
object get replaced rather than merged, and remember the shape of the
damage — it usually shows up in production as a lost settings sub-object.

## ex6 — contained by

`<@` with a literal on the right is the "all values drawn from this set"
test. It is the same operator as `@>` read backwards, and GIN indexes only
the `@>` direction, which is worth knowing before you build on it.

## ex7 — the three nothings

The table is tiny on purpose. The classification logic is what you are
building, and you will reuse it every time you inherit a document column
with inconsistent writers.

## ex8 — the key inventory

The first query to run against any undocumented jsonb column. Keep it.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — the
  storage model, containment rules and the scalar-in-array exception.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html)
  — the full operator table, including everything `-`, `#-` and `||` do.
- [TOAST](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/storage-toast.html) — why a
  wide document costs what it costs to read one key out of.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — which of
  these operators an index can actually answer.

or on `jsonb` equality, which is structural.

**Casting text out of a number and comparing it as text.** `payload ->>
'value' > '995'` compares strings, so `'99'` beats `'1000'`. Cast first.
Roughly a third of all "the filter returns the wrong rows" bug reports
against a document column are this.

only. For nesting, navigate first (`attributes -> 'meta' ? 'color'`) or
write a containment test that names the shape you want.

'{"a": {"y": 2}}'::jsonb` is `{"a": {"y": 2}}`. The nested `x` is gone.

fine, but it arrives through drivers that route JSON numbers via IEEE

with a delay fuse.

document and MVCC rewrites the whole row. A counter inside a document is
the most expensive counter you can build.

*"What is the difference between `json` and `jsonb`, and which do you
use?"*

cheap, every read reparses, key order and duplicates and whitespace are
preserved exactly. `jsonb` parses on insert into a binary form: keys are
sorted and deduplicated, whitespace is gone, reads are cheap, and — the
reason it wins — it supports containment and existence operators and can be
indexed with GIN. Use `jsonb`. Reach for `json` only when the exact bytes
are the point, such as a signed payload you must verify later.

Say that `@>` is recursive, that it searches inside arrays, that it ignores
array order and extra keys, that it is what GIN accelerates, and that its
top-level scalar-in-array case is the one asymmetry worth remembering. If
they push once more, the answer they are usually fishing for is the
write-amplification one: a document column turns a two-byte update into a
whole-row rewrite.

1. Why does `'{"a":1,"a":2}'::jsonb` have one key, and which value wins?
2. What does `jsonb_typeof(attributes -> 'nope')` return, and why is that
   not the string `'null'`?
3. Name the one operator that distinguishes a missing key from a key whose
   value is JSON `null`.

10. What is the difference between `#>` and `#>>`, and when does the
    difference bite?
11. How would you list every distinct top-level key in an undocumented
    jsonb column?
12. Why can two jsonb values be equal while their `::text` renderings
    differ?
13. Under what circumstances is `pg_column_size(doc)` larger than

The table is tiny on purpose. The classification logic is what you are
building, and you will reuse it every time you inherit a document column
with inconsistent writers.

## ex8 — the key inventory

The first query to run against any undocumented jsonb column. Keep it.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — the
  storage model, containment rules and the scalar-in-array exception.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html)
  — the full operator table, including everything `-`, `#-` and `||` do.
- [TOAST](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/storage-toast.html) — why a
  wide document costs what it costs to read one key out of.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — which of
  these operators an index can actually answer.

## How it works underneath

A `jsonb` value on disk is a varlena: a length header followed by a
recursive structure of *containers*. Each container is a header word
carrying a type tag and an element count, then an array of `JEntry` words,
then the payload bytes. A `JEntry` is 32 bits — a few type bits plus a
length or an offset. Objects store all their keys first and then all their
values, both in key-sort order, which is why lookup by key is a binary
search over the key entries rather than a scan of pairs.

That layout explains the behaviour you observe. Sorted keys are not a
stylistic choice, they are the index. Deduplication happens because the
parser builds a sorted key array and collapses equal keys as it goes.
Whitespace cannot survive because nothing in the layout has anywhere to put
it. And roughly every fourth `JEntry` stores an absolute offset rather than
a length — a compromise added in 9.5 so that long arrays stay
random-accessible without making every entry wider.

Scalars are stored as their PostgreSQL types: strings as bare bytes,
numbers as `numeric`. That is why a JSON number keeps thirty digits of
precision if you send thirty digits, and why arithmetic on values pulled
out of jsonb never surprises you the way JavaScript's does. It is also why
`numeric` overhead shows up in `pg_column_size` for documents full of small
integers, and why a tiny document can measure larger than its own text.

Because a jsonb value is a varlena it goes through TOAST like any other
wide value. Past roughly two kilobytes the whole document is compressed;
past roughly eight it is sliced into chunks in a side table. Both are
per-value and all-or-nothing: reading one key out of a 30 kB document
reads and decompresses all 30 kB. There is no partial detoast for jsonb,
and no amount of clever pathing avoids it.

## Historical context

PostgreSQL shipped `json` in 9.2 as little more than a validating text
type — enough to stop garbage getting in, not enough to query. The 9.3
release added the accessor operators. `jsonb` arrived in 9.4, borrowing
its container format from the `hstore` work that had come before it, and
it changed the conversation: suddenly a relational database could serve
document workloads without a second datastore. 9.5 added `||`, `-`, `#-`
and `jsonb_set`. Postgres 12 added the SQL/JSON path language, which the
next sector covers. Each step made the document column more capable, and
each step made it slightly easier to postpone the schema you should have
written.

## Performance notes

The single most important fact about writing jsonb: **every update
rewrites the entire value**. `jsonb_set(doc, '{status}', '"paid"')` builds
a whole new document, and MVCC then writes a whole new row version. On a
4 kB document that is 4 kB of new heap, 4 kB of WAL, and every index on the
table potentially touched. A column update of a two-byte integer is a
rounding error next to it. If a field changes often, it is not a document
field, it is a column.

Reads are cheap by comparison, with one asterisk. Key lookup inside a
container is a binary search, so wide objects are fine, but each `->` step
detoasts the value if it is stored out of line, and a chain of five arrows
across a `SELECT` list can pay that cost repeatedly. When a query extracts
several keys from the same wide document, extract once in a subquery or a
lateral and reuse the result.

Statistics are the quiet cost. The planner keeps no per-key histograms for
a document column. For `attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'` it falls back to
a fixed selectivity estimate, so cardinality guesses are frequently off by
an order of magnitude, and a join order chosen off the back of them can be
badly wrong. Extracting the two keys you filter on into real columns is not
only faster to read, it gives the planner numbers to work with. That is
lesson 36's argument about statistics, arriving from a new direction.

## When not to use it

A document column is the right answer for genuinely open-ended, sparse,
per-tenant or per-integration data whose shape you do not control: webhook
payloads, feature flags, third-party responses you archive verbatim,
user-defined form fields, the long tail of product attributes that differ
per category.

It is the wrong answer when any of the following holds. The keys are known
in advance and queried constantly — those are columns. A value needs a
foreign key — you cannot reference another table from inside a document. A
value needs a type guarantee — nothing stops `"quantity": "three"` landing
next to `"quantity": 3` in the same column, and you find out at read time,
in production, inside a cast. A value changes on a hot path — see the
rewrite cost above. Or the document is deeply nested and you find yourself
writing five-level paths: that is a schema hiding inside a string, and it
will be cheaper to normalise now than after another year of writes.

The honest summary is that jsonb buys you schema flexibility at write time
and charges you schema discipline at read time. That trade is excellent
when the write side genuinely cannot be pinned down, and terrible when it
can be and you simply did not want to write the migration.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — what type is that

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. For the ten products with `id <= 10`, report what
JSON type each attribute holds.

Return four columns in this order: `id`, `color_type`, `tags_type`,
`discount_type`, where each `*_type` is `jsonb_typeof` of the matching key
inside `attributes`. No product carries a `discount` key.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (10 rows.)

Expect rows shaped like `1 | string | array | NULL`. The last column is SQL
NULL, not the four-character string `null` — read that difference off the
output before you move on.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`jsonb_typeof` takes a `jsonb` value, not a key name. So you have to
navigate to the value first, and only one of the two arrow operators
returns something `jsonb_typeof` will accept.

## Hint 2

The shape is the same for each column:

```sql
SELECT id, jsonb_typeof(attributes -> 'size') AS size_type
FROM products WHERE id <= 3 ORDER BY id;
```

## Hint 3

Three of those, one per key, plus `id`, plus the filter and the ordering.
The only decision left is `->` versus `->>` — one of them returns text,
and `jsonb_typeof(text)` is a type error, so the error message will tell
you if you pick wrong.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the storage model. A jsonb container tags every value with its
type, so `jsonb_typeof` is a read of something already recorded, not an
inference. That is why it can answer `object` and `array`, which no text
inspection would give you cheaply.

## Hint 2

Ask what happens when the key is not there. The container has no entry, so
the operator has nothing to return, and "nothing to return" in SQL is NULL
— which is a value of the *SQL* type system, not of JSON's. That is why
`discount_type` comes back NULL rather than `'null'`.

## Hint 3

If your fourth column shows the text `null` instead of an empty cell, you
have accidentally produced a JSON null somewhere — most likely by wrapping
the missing lookup in a `coalesce` or by testing against a document that
actually has the key. Take the wrapping off and let the NULL through.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex1 — what type is that
SELECT id,
       jsonb_typeof(attributes -> 'color')    AS color_type,
       jsonb_typeof(attributes -> 'tags')     AS tags_type,
       jsonb_typeof(attributes -> 'discount') AS discount_type
FROM products
WHERE id <= 10
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex1 — path-operator formulation
SELECT id,
       jsonb_typeof(attributes #> '{color}')    AS color_type,
       jsonb_typeof(attributes #> '{tags}')     AS tags_type,
       jsonb_typeof(attributes #> '{discount}') AS discount_type
FROM products
WHERE id <= 10
ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — containment, not equality

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Count the products whose attributes say both
`"color": "red"` and `"size": "xl"`.

Return one row, one column named `matches`.

Write the predicate as a **single containment test** with `@>` against one
document literal — not as two `->>` comparisons joined by `AND`. Both give
the same answer here; only one of them is a single operator the GIN index
from lesson 42 can serve, and getting into the habit is the point of the
exercise.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Containment compares two documents. So the right-hand side of `@>` is not
two strings, it is one JSON object with two keys in it.

## Hint 2

A one-key version looks like this:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red"}';
```

Extra keys on the *left* are ignored by containment, which is why this
matches products that also carry a size and tags.

## Hint 3

Put both keys inside the same literal. Watch your quoting: the literal is a
single-quoted SQL string whose contents are JSON, so the JSON strings
inside it use double quotes. If PostgreSQL complains about the operator not
existing for `jsonb` and `unknown`, add an explicit `::jsonb` cast to the
literal.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the index. Lesson 42 said a GIN index over a document
column stores keys and values and answers containment by intersecting
posting lists. Ask yourself what that machinery can do with the expression
`attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'`, and the answer is: nothing at all, it
never sees a document.

## Hint 2

Now ask what the equivalent containment document looks like. GIN turns
`@> '{"color": "red", "size": "xl"}'` into two lookups and an
intersection. That tells you the right-hand side must be *one* document
carrying both facts, because two separate `@>` tests joined by `AND` would
be two index scans and a BitmapAnd instead.

## Hint 3

If you are unsure whether your literal parses, select it on its own first:
`SELECT '{"color": "red", "size": "xl"}'::jsonb;`. If that returns a
document, the predicate will work; if it raises, the problem is quoting,
not containment.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex2 — containment, not equality
SELECT count(*) AS matches
FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red", "size": "xl"}'::jsonb;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex2 — the extract-and-compare formulation
SELECT count(*) AS matches
FROM products
WHERE attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'
  AND attributes ->> 'size'  = 'xl';

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — does the key exist

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Every product is supposed to carry all three
attribute keys: `color`, `size` and `tags`. Verify it.

Return one row with two columns, in this order:

- `complete` — how many products have **all three** keys
- `total` — how many products there are

Use a key-existence operator, not `->>` and not `@>`: the question is
whether the keys are present, and a value's content is irrelevant to it.

Expect `complete` to equal `total`. A schema claim you have never checked
is a schema claim you do not have.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three operators test key existence: one key, any of a list, all of a list.
You want the third.

## Hint 2

The "any of" form reads like this:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM products
WHERE attributes ?| array['color', 'discount'];
```

The right-hand side is a `text[]`, which is why it is written with
`array[...]` and not as a JSON array.

## Hint 3

Swap the operator for the all-of variant and list all three keys. Getting
both counts into one row without a join is the second half of the exercise:
`count(*)` counts every row, and a filtered count counts a subset of the
same scan.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what a GIN index with the default `jsonb_ops` operator class
stores: every key as its own entry, and every value as its own entry.
Existence questions are answerable from the key entries alone. That is the
category of question you are being asked to write.

## Hint 2

Two aggregates over one scan is a `FILTER` clause, which lesson 17 covered:
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE <predicate>)` counts only the rows where the
predicate holds, alongside a plain `count(*)` in the same select list.

## Hint 3

If you write it as two subqueries instead, it is still correct — but read
the plan afterwards and count the scans. One scan producing two aggregates
is the shape to prefer, and on ten thousand rows the difference is
invisible while the habit is not.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex3 — does the key exist
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE attributes ?& array['color', 'size', 'tags'])
         AS complete,
       count(*) AS total
FROM products;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex3 — the two-scalar-subquery formulation
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM products
        WHERE attributes ? 'color'
          AND attributes ? 'size'
          AND attributes ? 'tags') AS complete,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM products) AS total;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — subtraction

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. For the five products with `id <= 5`, show what
the attributes would look like with the noise removed.

Return three columns in this order:

- `id`
- `without_tags` — `attributes` with the top-level `tags` key deleted
- `first_tag_dropped` — `attributes` with only the **first element** of the
  `tags` array removed, the rest of the document untouched

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (5 rows.)

So a product holding `{"color": "red", "size": "xl", "tags": ["eco",
"limited"]}` yields `{"color": "red", "size": "xl"}` in the second column
and `{"color": "red", "size": "xl", "tags": ["limited"]}` in the third.

Neither column changes the stored row. After the gate passes, run
`SELECT attributes FROM products WHERE id = 1;` in the lab and confirm it.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two different deletions: one names a key, the other names a position inside
a nested array. PostgreSQL has one operator for each, and the second one
takes a path rather than a name.

## Hint 2

Deleting at a path looks like this:

```sql
SELECT '{"a": {"b": [10, 20]}}'::jsonb #- '{a,b,1}';
-- {"a": {"b": [10]}}
```

The path is a `text[]` literal, and array positions inside it are
zero-based.

## Hint 3

The first column is the single-key delete operator with `'tags'` on the
right. The second is the path delete, with a two-element path naming the
array and then the element. Decide for yourself whether the element index
you want is `0` or `1`, and check it against the example in the prompt.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a value question. `attributes - 'tags'` is an expression
like `price * 2`: it computes something new out of an input and hands it
back. Nothing about it is a statement, and nothing about it touches the
table. Once that clicks, the exercise is just two expressions in a select
list.

## Hint 2

The failure you are most likely to hit is a type one. The `-` operator is
overloaded on the right-hand side: `text` deletes a key, `integer` deletes
an array element, `text[]` deletes several keys. If you pass an integer to
a document whose top level is an object, you get an error rather than the
result you wanted — the top level here is an object, so the integer form
is not available to you.

## Hint 3

If you try to reach the array element with the `-` operator by chaining
(`attributes -> 'tags' - 0`), you will get a correct *array*, not a correct
*document* — you have thrown away colour and size. The path-deleting
operator exists precisely so you can remove something deep and keep
everything else.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex4 — subtraction
SELECT id,
       attributes - 'tags'      AS without_tags,
       attributes #- '{tags,0}' AS first_tag_dropped
FROM products
WHERE id <= 5
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex4 — rebuilt rather than subtracted
SELECT id,
       jsonb_build_object('color', attributes -> 'color',
                          'size',  attributes -> 'size') AS without_tags,
       jsonb_set(attributes, '{tags}',
                 (attributes -> 'tags') - 0)             AS first_tag_dropped
FROM products
WHERE id <= 5
ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — merge is shallow

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Two questions in one result set, and the second is
the one that matters.

Return one row with three columns, in this order:

- `flagged` — the document `{"color": "red"}` merged with
  `{"clearance": true}`, using `||`
- `deep_target` — the literal document
  `{"meta": {"source": "erp", "checked": true}}` merged with
  `{"meta": {"source": "csv"}}`, using `||`
- `lost_key` — boolean: is the key `checked` still present inside
  `deep_target -> 'meta'`?

Write the literals inline; no table is involved.

`flagged` comes back with two keys. `deep_target` comes back with one key
whose value has one key, and `lost_key` comes back false. Predict all three
before you run it, then look at what `||` did to the nested object.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`||` between two objects produces an object whose keys are the union, with
the right-hand side winning every collision. Ask what "winning" means when
the colliding value is itself an object.

## Hint 2

For the third column you need a key-existence test applied to a nested
value, which means navigating first:

```sql
SELECT ('{"m": {"a": 1}}'::jsonb -> 'm') ? 'a';   -- true
```

## Hint 3

Compute the merged document once and ask the existence question of it. You
can repeat the whole `||` expression in the third column, or name it once
in a `FROM (VALUES ...)` or a CTE and refer to it twice — the second is
what you would do in real code, and the gate accepts either.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what `||` can possibly know. It receives two containers. To
merge nested objects recursively it would have to decide, for every
colliding key, whether the two sides are "the same kind of thing" and
whether merging or replacing is meant. There is no way for the operator to
know that, so it does the only unambiguous thing: replace.

## Hint 2

That is the same decision `jsonb_set` makes at a path, and the same one
`hstore`'s merge made before jsonb existed. Every document store that
offers a deep merge also offers a pile of configuration about how arrays
are treated, which is the tell that there is no single right answer.

## Hint 3

If your third column comes back true, check which document you asked. The
question is about `checked` inside the *merged* value, not inside the
original literal — the original still has it, which is exactly why the loss
is easy to miss in a code review.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex5 — merge is shallow
WITH merged AS (
  SELECT '{"color": "red"}'::jsonb || '{"clearance": true}'::jsonb
           AS flagged,
         '{"meta": {"source": "erp", "checked": true}}'::jsonb
           || '{"meta": {"source": "csv"}}'::jsonb
           AS deep_target
)
SELECT flagged,
       deep_target,
       (deep_target -> 'meta') ? 'checked' AS lost_key
FROM merged;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex5 — the same three answers without a CTE
SELECT '{"color": "red"}'::jsonb || '{"clearance": true}'::jsonb AS flagged,
       '{"meta": {"source": "erp", "checked": true}}'::jsonb
         || '{"meta": {"source": "csv"}}'::jsonb AS deep_target,
       jsonb_path_exists(
         '{"meta": {"source": "erp", "checked": true}}'::jsonb
           || '{"meta": {"source": "csv"}}'::jsonb,
         '$.meta.checked') AS lost_key;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — contained by

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Every product carries exactly two distinct tags.
Find the ones whose tags are drawn entirely from the pair `eco` and
`limited` — that is, both of a product's tags are in that set.

Return two columns, `id` and `name`, **ordered by `id` ascending**.

Use `<@` on the tags array. Note that `@>` cannot phrase this question:
`attributes @> '{"tags": ["eco", "limited"]}'` asks whether the product has
*at least* those two tags, which is a different claim about a different set
of rows — here the two happen to select the same products, and you should
be able to say why before you write either.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`<@` is `@>` with the arguments swapped. So the value you are asking about
goes on the left and the set that must contain it goes on the right.

## Hint 2

Containment on arrays is a subset test that ignores order and duplicates:

```sql
SELECT '["b","a"]'::jsonb <@ '["a","b","c"]'::jsonb;   -- true
```

## Hint 3

Navigate to the tags array first, then apply the operator against a JSON
array literal holding the two allowed tags. Decide whether you want the
whole document or just the array on the left — only one of them can be a
subset of a bare array.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the index can do here. Lesson 42's GIN index accelerates the `@>`
direction; `<@` is not in the operator class, so a query written this way
scans. On ten thousand products that is fine, and knowing it is fine is
part of the skill — but do not carry the pattern to the three-million-row
events table without measuring.

## Hint 2

There is a second phrasing that is indexable, and it works only because of
a fact about this data: each product has exactly two tags. If a product has
two tags and both are in a two-element set, it has *precisely* that set —
so `@> '{"tags": ["eco", "limited"]}'` selects the same rows here. That
equivalence is data-dependent, and it evaporates the day a product gets a
third tag.

## Hint 3

Write the `<@` version for the gate, then run the `@>` version in the lab
and compare row counts. Then imagine a product tagged `eco` alone: predict
which of the two queries returns it before you test it.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex6 — contained by
SELECT id, name
FROM products
WHERE attributes -> 'tags' <@ '["eco", "limited"]'::jsonb
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex6 — every element checked individually
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS t(tag)
        WHERE t.tag NOT IN ('eco', 'limited'))
ORDER BY p.id;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — the three nothings

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Build the classification that tells a missing key,
a JSON null and a SQL NULL apart.

Work from this exact input, inline — no table is created:

```sql
(VALUES (1, '{"discount": 10}'::jsonb),
        (2, '{"discount": null}'::jsonb),
        (3, '{}'::jsonb),
        (4, NULL::jsonb)) AS t(id, doc)
```

Return four columns in this order, ordered by `id` ascending (4 rows):

- `id`
- `has_key` — boolean: does `doc` have a top-level `discount` key
- `value_type` — `jsonb_typeof` of the discount value
- `verdict` — text, one of `present`, `json_null`, `missing`, `no_document`

The verdicts map like this: row 1 is `present`, row 2 is `json_null`, row 3
is `missing`, row 4 is `no_document`. Note that `has_key` for row 4 is
NULL, not false: an operator applied to SQL NULL returns SQL NULL, which is
the third nothing showing you where it lives.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Order your `CASE` branches by how much they know. The outermost question is
whether there is a document at all; only then can you ask about keys.

## Hint 2

The three tests you need, one per branch:

```sql
doc IS NULL                       -- no document
doc ? 'discount'                  -- key present (of either kind)
jsonb_typeof(doc -> 'discount')   -- 'null' when the value is JSON null
```

## Hint 3

A `CASE` whose first branch is the SQL NULL test, whose second is the
key-existence test, and whose third distinguishes the two kinds of present
key. You get to choose whether the JSON-null branch tests the type string
or tests `->>` for NULL while `?` is true — both work, and they fail
differently on documents you have not seen yet.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from where each nothing lives. The SQL NULL lives in the *column*:
the row has no document. The missing key lives in the *container*: there is
a document, it has no such entry. The JSON null lives in the *value*: there
is an entry, and its content is the JSON literal null. Three levels, three
tests.

## Hint 2

This matters because the three come from different writers. A missing key
usually means an older application version. A JSON null usually means a
client that serialises its optional fields explicitly. A SQL NULL usually
means the column was never written at all. When you inherit a document
column, the mix of the three is a history of the code that wrote it.

## Hint 3

Watch out for the trap in `CASE`: a branch whose condition evaluates to
NULL is not taken, and falls through to `ELSE`. So if you test
`WHEN doc ? 'discount' THEN ...` first, row 4 does not match it, does not
match a later branch either, and lands in whatever your `ELSE` says. Put
the `IS NULL` test first, or make your `ELSE` the honest one.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex7 — the three nothings
SELECT id,
       doc ? 'discount'                AS has_key,
       jsonb_typeof(doc -> 'discount') AS value_type,
       CASE
         WHEN doc IS NULL                            THEN 'no_document'
         WHEN NOT doc ? 'discount'                   THEN 'missing'
         WHEN jsonb_typeof(doc -> 'discount') = 'null' THEN 'json_null'
         ELSE 'present'
       END AS verdict
FROM (VALUES (1, '{"discount": 10}'::jsonb),
             (2, '{"discount": null}'::jsonb),
             (3, '{}'::jsonb),
             (4, NULL::jsonb)) AS t(id, doc)
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex7 — driven off the extracted text instead
SELECT id,
       doc ? 'discount'                AS has_key,
       jsonb_typeof(doc -> 'discount') AS value_type,
       CASE
         WHEN doc IS NULL                                 THEN 'no_document'
         WHEN doc ? 'discount' AND doc ->> 'discount' IS NOT NULL
                                                          THEN 'present'
         WHEN doc ? 'discount'                            THEN 'json_null'
         ELSE 'missing'
       END AS verdict
FROM (VALUES (1, '{"discount": 10}'::jsonb),
             (2, '{"discount": null}'::jsonb),
             (3, '{}'::jsonb),
             (4, NULL::jsonb)) AS t(id, doc)
ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the key inventory

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. You have inherited a document column and no
documentation. Write the query that describes it.

For the first two hundred products (`id <= 200`), explode `attributes` into
key/value pairs and report, per top-level key:

- `key` — the key name
- `rows` — how many of the two hundred products carry it
- `distinct_values` — how many distinct values it takes
- `value_types` — the distinct `jsonb_typeof` values it holds, as a
  comma-separated text list in alphabetical order

**Ordered by `key` ascending.** (3 rows — `color`, `size`, `tags`.)

`tags` will report one type (`array`) and a large number of distinct
values, because each distinct pair of tags is a distinct array. That is
the signal you are looking for in this report: a key whose distinct count
tracks the row count is data, and a key with five distinct values is an
enum somebody forgot to declare.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You cannot group by a key until each key is a row. There is a
set-returning function that turns one document into one row per top-level
pair, and it comes in a jsonb-valued and a text-valued flavour — you want
the one that keeps the value as `jsonb`, because you still need its type.

## Hint 2

Set-returning functions go in `FROM`, beside the table, and may reference
its columns:

```sql
SELECT e.key, count(*)
FROM products p, jsonb_each(p.attributes) AS e(key, value)
GROUP BY e.key;
```

## Hint 3

From there it is one `GROUP BY` with three aggregates. Two are counts —
one of rows, one of distinct values. The third collects distinct type
names into a sorted list, which is a string aggregate with `DISTINCT` and
an `ORDER BY` inside the call.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what this report is *for*. You are reconstructing a schema from
data, so the questions are the ones a schema would have answered: is the key
always present, is the value always the same type, how many values does it
take. Each of those is one aggregate.

## Hint 2

The type column is the interesting one and the one people skip. A key that
reports `number,string` in a real system means two writers disagreed, and
every cast you have downstream is a time bomb. Getting a *sorted*
comma-separated list matters because you want to diff this report between
environments.

## Hint 3

`string_agg(DISTINCT jsonb_typeof(value), ',' ORDER BY jsonb_typeof(value))`
is the shape. PostgreSQL requires that when you combine `DISTINCT` with
`ORDER BY` inside an aggregate, the ordering expression matches the
distinct expression — if you order by something else, it will tell you so
rather than guess.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex8 — the key inventory
SELECT e.key AS key,
       count(*) AS rows,
       count(DISTINCT e.value) AS distinct_values,
       string_agg(DISTINCT jsonb_typeof(e.value), ','
                  ORDER BY jsonb_typeof(e.value)) AS value_types
FROM products p,
     jsonb_each(p.attributes) AS e(key, value)
WHERE p.id <= 200
GROUP BY e.key
ORDER BY e.key;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / ex8 — keys and values gathered separately
WITH pairs AS (
  SELECT k.key,
         p.attributes -> k.key AS value
  FROM products p,
       jsonb_object_keys(p.attributes) AS k(key)
  WHERE p.id <= 200
)
SELECT key,
       count(*)                AS rows,
       count(DISTINCT value)   AS distinct_values,
       (SELECT string_agg(t, ',' ORDER BY t)
        FROM (SELECT DISTINCT jsonb_typeof(p2.value) AS t
              FROM pairs p2
              WHERE p2.key = pairs.key) s) AS value_types
FROM pairs
GROUP BY key
ORDER BY key;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — normalise a document

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants a flattened export
document per product: no tag noise, a price band computed server-side, and
the source data kept.

For the products with `id <= 50` **whose attributes contain `"color":
"red"`**, return two columns:

- `id`
- `export` — a `jsonb` document built from `attributes` by
  1. deleting the `tags` key,
  2. adding a `price_band` key whose value is the text `low` when `price`
     is under 50, `mid` when it is under 200, and `high` otherwise,
  3. adding a `tag_count` key whose value is a JSON **number**: how many
     tags the product had before you deleted them.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

A product priced 129.00, coloured red, size `xl`, tagged `eco` and
`limited` produces:

```json
{"size": "xl", "color": "red", "tag_count": 2, "price_band": "mid"}
```

Key order in the output does not matter — jsonb sorts keys itself, and the
gate compares documents structurally, not as text.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three operations compose into one expression: a deletion, and a merge that
adds two keys at once. Build the two added keys as a single document rather
than merging twice.

## Hint 2

`jsonb_build_object` takes alternating keys and values and gets the JSON
types right for you:

```sql
SELECT jsonb_build_object('n', 2, 'label', 'mid');
-- {"n": 2, "label": "mid"}
```

Note that `2` becomes a JSON number and `'mid'` a JSON string, because the
SQL types were `integer` and `text`.

## Hint 3

The skeleton is `(attributes - 'tags') || jsonb_build_object(...)`. Inside
the build, the band is a `CASE` over `price` and the count is a length
function applied to the tags array — decide whether you take that length
before or after the deletion, because only one order works.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Watch the JSON types. If you build the count with `(attributes ->
'tags')::text` or wrap it in `to_char`, you get a JSON *string* and the
gate will reject it. JSON distinguishes `2` from `"2"` and so does the
comparison.

## Hint 2

There are two functions that measure a JSON array. One returns the number
of elements of a jsonb array; the other counts rows after expanding it.
The first is a scalar expression you can drop straight into
`jsonb_build_object`; the second needs a subquery. Prefer the scalar.

## Hint 3

For the filter, resist writing `attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'` — you now
know the containment spelling, and this is the query where it pays, because
`id <= 50` and a containment test are exactly the two predicates a bitmap
plan combines. Write the containment form and read the plan afterwards.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / challenge — normalise a document
SELECT id,
       (attributes - 'tags')
         || jsonb_build_object(
              'price_band',
              CASE WHEN price < 50  THEN 'low'
                   WHEN price < 200 THEN 'mid'
                   ELSE 'high' END,
              'tag_count',
              jsonb_array_length(attributes -> 'tags')) AS export
FROM products
WHERE id <= 50
  AND attributes @> '{"color": "red"}'
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / challenge — assembled key by key
SELECT id,
       jsonb_build_object('color', attributes -> 'color',
                          'size',  attributes -> 'size')
         || jsonb_build_object('price_band',
                               CASE WHEN price < 50  THEN 'low'
                                    WHEN price < 200 THEN 'mid'
                                    ELSE 'high' END)
         || jsonb_build_object('tag_count',
                               (SELECT count(*)
                                FROM jsonb_array_elements(
                                       attributes -> 'tags'))) AS export
FROM products
WHERE id <= 50
  AND attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'
ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the same question two ways

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. The clickstream payload looks like
`{"path": "/p/4242", "value": 618}`, and `value` runs from 0 to 1000.

Count the events whose value is exactly 1000, twice in one query, and prove
the two counts agree.

Return one row with three columns, in this order:

- `by_containment` — the count computed with `payload @> '{"value": 1000}'`
- `by_extract` — the count computed with `(payload ->> 'value')::int = 1000`
- `agree` — boolean, whether the two counts are equal

Then, in the lab, run a third version: `payload ->> 'value' = '1000'`
without the cast, and a fourth: `payload ->> 'value' > '995'`. The third
agrees; the fourth does not, and its disagreement is the whole reason this
review exists.

```
uv run dojo test v3c01_jsonb_storage review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two counts over the same table in one row is a job for two filtered
aggregates over one scan, not for two separate queries stitched together.

## Hint 2

A filtered count looks like this:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'view') AS views,
       count(*) AS total
FROM events;
```

## Hint 3

Two of those with the two different predicates, then a third column
comparing them. The comparison cannot reference the output column names in
the same select list, so either repeat the expressions or wrap the two
counts in a subquery and compare in the outer one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the types. `payload @> '{"value": 1000}'` compares a JSON number
to a JSON number inside the container — no cast, no text. `(payload ->>
'value')::int = 1000` extracts text and converts it. Two different type
systems answering the same question, and the exercise is really asking
whether you trust them to agree.

## Hint 2

They agree here because every value in this dataset is an integer written
without a decimal point or leading zeros. They would stop agreeing the
moment a writer sent `1000.0`: containment would see a different JSON
number and the cast would see the same integer. Containment is exact on
JSON values; the cast normalises. Neither is wrong, and knowing which one
you want is the skill.

## Hint 3

If the cast version errors with "invalid input syntax for type integer",
you have found a payload where `value` is not a number at all, and you have
just discovered the argument for the next sector's `jsonb_path_query` with
its type-aware filters. On this dataset it will not happen; on yours it
will.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / review1 — the same question two ways
SELECT c.by_containment,
       c.by_extract,
       c.by_containment = c.by_extract AS agree
FROM (
  SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE payload @> '{"value": 1000}')
           AS by_containment,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE (payload ->> 'value')::int = 1000)
           AS by_extract
  FROM events
) c;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c01_jsonb_storage / review1 — two scalar subqueries, compared outside
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM events
          WHERE payload @> '{"value": 1000}') AS by_containment,
         (SELECT count(*) FROM events
          WHERE (payload ->> 'value')::int = 1000) AS by_extract
)
SELECT by_containment,
       by_extract,
       by_containment IS NOT DISTINCT FROM by_extract AS agree
FROM counts;

lessons.title: V3·C2 — Nested JSONB: paths, updates and aggregation
lessons.summary: Arrows run out of road once documents nest and filter conditions live inside arrays. This sector picks up the SQL/JSON path language, the jsonb_set family that rebuilds documents, and the aggregates that assemble them, including the lax-mode rule that silently swallows the errors you wanted to see.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·C2 — Nested JSONB: paths, updates and aggregation

The previous sector's operators are enough for flat documents. They run out
the moment nesting appears. Ask "does this order contain a line item with
quantity above ten" and the arrow toolkit has no answer: you can navigate to
the array, but you cannot express a condition *inside* it without exploding
it into rows first. And once you want to write rather than read, the arrows
offer nothing at all — there is no assignment operator for a document.

PostgreSQL 12 imported the SQL/JSON path language from the SQL:2016
standard to solve the first problem, and 9.5 added the `jsonb_set` family
to solve the second. This sector is about both, plus the aggregates that
turn query results back into documents. Together they are the difference
between reading a document column and working in one.

## Concept

A path expression is a small language of its own, written inside a string
of type `jsonpath`:

```sql
SELECT jsonb_path_query(
         '{"items": [{"sku": "a", "qty": 3}, {"sku": "b", "qty": 12}]}',
         '$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 10)');
-- {"sku": "b", "qty": 12}
```

`$` is the document, `.key` navigates, `[*]` iterates an array, `[0]` picks
an element, and `? (...)` is a filter whose `@` refers to the item under
test. Inside a filter you get comparisons, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `exists(...)`,
`like_regex`, `starts with`, and the accessors `.type()`, `.size()`,
`.double()`.

Four ways to run one:

```sql
jsonb_path_query(doc, path)        -- setof jsonb: every match
jsonb_path_query_first(doc, path)  -- jsonb: the first match or NULL
jsonb_path_query_array(doc, path)  -- jsonb: all matches wrapped in an array
jsonb_path_exists(doc, path)       -- boolean: did anything match
```

and two operators that are the indexable spellings of the last one:

```sql
payload @? '$.value ? (@ > 995)'   -- path finds something
payload @@ '$.value > 995'         -- path *predicate* is true
```

Both are supported by a default GIN index — which is the reason to prefer
the operators over the function calls in a `WHERE` clause.

The trap is **lax mode**, which is the default. In lax mode the engine
adapts to the document: it unwraps arrays when you address them as scalars,
wraps scalars when you iterate them, and — the part that hurts — returns no
rows instead of raising when the path does not fit the document. Prefix the
path with `strict` and the same mismatch becomes an error:

```sql
SELECT jsonb_path_query('{"a": 1}', 'strict $.a[*]');
-- ERROR:  jsonpath array accessor can only be applied to an array
SELECT jsonb_path_query('{"a": 1}', 'lax $.a[*]');
-- 1
```

Lax is right for exploratory work across documents whose shape varies.
Strict is right when a mismatch means a bug and you would rather hear about
it.

Writing is a separate toolkit, and none of it mutates:

```sql
jsonb_set(doc, '{meta,source}', '"csv"')          -- replace at a path
jsonb_set(doc, '{meta,source}', '"csv"', false)   -- and do not create it
jsonb_insert(doc, '{tags,0}', '"new"')            -- insert before element 0
jsonb_insert(doc, '{tags,0}', '"new"', true)      -- insert after it
doc #- '{meta,source}'                            -- delete at a path
jsonb_strip_nulls(doc)                            -- drop JSON-null members
```

`jsonb_set`'s third argument is `jsonb`, not text — `'"csv"'` with the
inner quotes, or `to_jsonb('csv'::text)`. Its fourth argument defaults to
true, meaning a missing key gets created; pass `false` when you mean
"update if present, otherwise leave alone", which is usually what a
migration wants.

And going the other way, aggregates build documents out of rows:

```sql
jsonb_agg(x)                  -- rows -> array, honours ORDER BY inside
jsonb_object_agg(k, v)        -- pairs -> object
jsonb_build_object('a', 1)    -- alternating keys and values, types kept
to_jsonb(t)                   -- a whole row -> an object, column names kept
```

## Exercise 1 — the path, by path

Replace an arrow chain with `jsonb_path_query_first`, and see what the two
return differently when the key is absent.

## Exercise 2 — a filter inside an array

Find products whose tag list satisfies a condition, expressed as a filter
inside the path rather than as an explosion into rows.

## Exercise 3 — the indexable spelling

Count clickstream events above a threshold with `@?`, and then with `@@`,
and note which one takes a predicate and which takes a path.

## Exercise 4 — lax and strict

Four documents of inconsistent shape, one path, two modes. You will build
the table that shows exactly what lax mode hides.

## Exercise 5 — set, with and without creation

`jsonb_set` twice over the same document: once on a key that exists, once
on a key that does not, with the create flag on and off.

## Exercise 6 — insert is not set

`jsonb_insert` adds an array element without replacing one. The exercise
makes the difference visible by doing both to the same array.

## Exercise 7 — build a document out of rows

`jsonb_object_agg` over a grouped query, producing one document that a
dashboard can consume without a second round trip.

## Exercise 8 — documents back into rows, typed

`jsonb_to_recordset` turns an array of objects into a typed relation you
can aggregate. This is the direction that lets a document column
participate in ordinary SQL.

## Challenge — a customer document

Assemble a nested document per customer: their details, an array of their
orders, each with an array of its line items. One query, three levels, no
application code.

## Review 1 — an actual update

Everything above computes documents. This one stores them: create a table,
write a nested key with `jsonb_set`, and report what changed. Then think
about how many bytes that cost.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3c02_jsonb_nested

The path language and the setter family come from opposite directions. One
is a standardised query sublanguage bolted onto a type; the other is a pile
of pragmatic functions that predate it. Knowing which is which explains
most of their inconsistencies.

## Notes

**A `jsonpath` is a value with its own type.** `'$.a[*] ? (@ > 3)'` parses
into a `jsonpath` value, and you can cast, store and parameterise it. That
also means syntax errors surface at parse time with a caret pointing at the
offending token, which is more than the arrow operators ever gave you.

**`$` is the document, `@` is the item under test.** Inside a filter the
context switches to whatever the filter is being applied to, which is why
`$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 10)` reads the way it does: iterate items, and for
each one, test its own `qty`.

**Lax mode is a compatibility layer, not a convenience.** It exists because
JSON documents in the wild are inconsistent: sometimes a field is a scalar,
sometimes an array of one. Lax mode auto-unwraps and auto-wraps so one path
serves both. The cost is that a path which simply does not fit returns zero
rows rather than an error, and zero rows looks exactly like "no match".
When you are debugging a path that returns nothing, rerun it with `strict`
before you rewrite it.

**`@?` and `@@` differ in what they take.** `@?` takes a path and asks
whether it yields anything: `payload @? '$.value ? (@ > 995)'`. `@@` takes
a path *predicate* and asks whether it is true: `payload @@ '$.value >
995'`. Both are GIN-indexable with the default operator class; the function
forms `jsonb_path_exists` and `jsonb_path_match` are not, which is the only
reason the operators exist.

**`jsonb_set` replaces, `jsonb_insert` inserts.** Setting an array element
overwrites it; inserting shifts the rest along. `jsonb_insert` refuses to
overwrite an existing object key — it raises rather than silently
replacing, which is the safer default for the operation it names.

**The create-if-missing flag is the migration flag.** `jsonb_set(doc,
path, value, false)` updates only documents that already have the key.
That is what you want when backfilling a rename, and the difference between
touching every row and touching the rows that need it.

**`jsonb_set` with a SQL NULL value returns NULL.** The whole document
becomes NULL, silently destroying it in an `UPDATE`. `jsonb_set_lax` exists
for exactly this: its fifth argument chooses between raising, writing a
JSON null, deleting the key, or returning the target unchanged. If a value
you are setting can be NULL, use it.

**Paths in the setter family are `text[]`, not `jsonpath`.** `'{meta,
source}'` is a two-element text array, and array indexes inside it are
written as numbers that count from zero, with negative numbers counting
from the end. The two path notations in one type are a historical accident
you simply have to keep straight.

**`jsonb_agg` orders like any aggregate.** `jsonb_agg(x ORDER BY y)` is
legal and is how you build an array with a defined order. Without the
`ORDER BY` the array order is the order rows happened to arrive, which is
a plan detail and will change under you.

**`json_agg` versus `jsonb_agg`.** If the result is being serialised
straight to a client and never queried, `json_agg` skips the parse into
binary form and is measurably cheaper. If anything downstream needs to
index, compare or navigate it, `jsonb_agg` is correct.

**Set-returning and record-returning functions.** `jsonb_array_elements`
gives you rows of jsonb; `jsonb_to_recordset(doc) AS x(a int, b text)`
gives you rows of *typed columns*, with the column list supplied by you
because a document carries no schema for the planner to read.

## ex1 — the path, by path

Note what `jsonb_path_query_first` does with an absent key: NULL, quietly,
in lax mode. That is the same answer the arrow gives, arrived at by a
different route.

## ex2 — a filter inside an array

The filter version reads the array without exploding it, which matters when
the array is long and the predicate is selective.

## ex3 — the indexable spelling

Run both under `EXPLAIN` with a GIN index on `payload` present. The
operator forms produce a bitmap index scan; wrap the same test in
`jsonb_path_exists(...)` and watch the plan fall back to a sequential scan.

## ex4 — lax and strict

The exercise you will remember in six months when a path returns nothing
and you cannot see why.

## ex5 — set, with and without creation

Two calls, one flag, four outcomes. Write out the four before you run it.

## ex6 — insert is not set

Also worth trying in the lab: `jsonb_insert` at a path naming an existing
object key, and read the error message.

## ex7 — build a document out of rows

One row out of a query that would otherwise be a hundred, which is often
the whole point of a document-shaped API response.

## ex8 — documents back into rows, typed

The column definition list is you supplying the schema the document does
not have. If a document holds `"qty": "3"`, this is where you find out.

## Further reading

- [SQL/JSON Path Language](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html#FUNCTIONS-SQLJSON-PATH)
  — the grammar, the filter operators, and the lax/strict rules in full.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html)
  — `jsonb_set`, `jsonb_insert`, `jsonb_set_lax`, and the aggregate family.
- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — the
  containment and existence semantics the operators build on.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html)
  — `jsonb_agg` and `jsonb_object_agg` alongside every other aggregate,
  including the `ORDER BY` clause they accept.

## Exercise 2 — a filter inside an array
