- [Row and Array Comparisons](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparisons.html)
  — `ANY`, `ALL`, and how NULL elements change the answer.

## How it works underneath

An array value is a varlena with a small header: the number of dimensions,
a null bitmap flag, the element type OID, then per-dimension lengths and
lower bounds, then the elements laid end to end. Two consequences follow
directly. Elements of a fixed-width type can be addressed by arithmetic, so
`arr[500]` on an `int[]` is cheap. Elements of a variable-width type such as
`text` cannot, so `arr[500]` on a `text[]` walks the first 499 elements. An
array of long strings is a linked list wearing an index's clothing.

The lower bound is stored per dimension, which is why arrays are one-based
by convention rather than by law: `'[5:7]={a,b,c}'::text[]` is a legal
array whose first index is 5. You will almost never see one, but the
storage supports it, and `array_lower`/`array_upper` exist because of it.

NULL elements are recorded in a null bitmap, which is why an array can
distinguish `{NULL}` from `{}` from NULL-the-column. Three empties again,
exactly like the JSONB sector's three nothings, and worth lining up
side by side once.

GIN indexing of arrays works the same way it does for JSONB: each distinct
element becomes an index key pointing at a posting list of rows.
Containment and overlap become intersections and unions of posting lists.
This is why `&&` and `@>` are fast and `arr[1] = 'x'` is not — position is
not part of the key, so an inverted index has nothing to offer it.

## Historical context

Arrays are in PostgreSQL because they were in POSTGRES, the research system,
in the 1980s. They predate the SQL standard's own array support, which
arrived in SQL:1999 and which PostgreSQL only partially follows. That
history explains the inconsistencies: the literal syntax has two forms
(`ARRAY[1,2]` and `'{1,2}'`), functions are named with a `array_` prefix
rather than following any standard, and the multidimensional model is
rectangular because it was designed for scientific data rather than for
nested records.

It also explains why arrays are so deeply woven into the rest of the
system. `?|` and `?&` on JSONB take `text[]`. The `text[]` path arguments
to `jsonb_set` are arrays. `VARIADIC` functions receive arrays. Statistics
about a column's most common values are stored in arrays inside
`pg_statistic`. Learning arrays well pays off in places that have nothing
to do with array columns.

## Performance notes

Deriving arrays per row is the cost people miss. `ARRAY(SELECT
jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags'))` allocates an array for
every row scanned, and on three million rows that is three million
allocations before any filter applies. If a derived array appears in a
`WHERE` clause on a large table, either store it as a column with a GIN
index or express the predicate against the source directly.

Unnesting multiplies rows before the planner's estimates get a chance to be
right. A table of a million rows with a five-element array becomes five
million rows, and the planner's guess about how many survive the subsequent
filter is usually poor because it has no statistics about array elements.
Unnest late, filter early — and where possible, filter with `&&` or `@>`
against the array before unnesting it, so the expansion happens on the rows
that matter.

`array_agg` builds its result in memory in one backend. Aggregating a
million values into one array is a memory spike and a single point of
failure, and the resulting value goes through TOAST on the way out. The
same rule as JSONB aggregation applies: aggregate when the array is the
answer, not when it is an intermediate.

## When not to use it

Do not model a relationship with an array of foreign keys. This is the
single most common misuse and it is not close. You lose referential
integrity, cascading deletes, per-element statistics, the ability to store
anything about the relationship itself, and the ability to join without
unnesting. What you gain is one fewer table in the diagram. That trade has
never been worth it in a system that lived more than a year.

Do not use an array to avoid a normalisation you find tedious. The moment
the elements acquire attributes — a date, an author, an order that means
something — you need rows, and converting an array column to a table under
load is more work than creating the table would have been.

Do not use arrays for long lists. Variable-width element access is linear,
TOAST compresses and decompresses the whole thing, and updating one element
rewrites the entire value exactly as JSONB does.

Do use them for small, closed, row-owned lists where the whole array is
read and written together: a set of flags, a fixed-length rubric, a
denormalised copy of tags maintained beside the real join table for fast
`&&` filtering. That last pattern — array as a maintained index, table as
the truth — is the mature version of the design, and it is worth knowing
that it exists before you argue for either extreme.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — indexing, slicing, measuring

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Establish the three facts about array mechanics
that everything else in this sector depends on.

Work from this exact input, inline:

```sql
(VALUES (1, ARRAY['eco', 'limited', 'recycled']),
        (2, ARRAY['sale']),
        (3, ARRAY[]::text[])) AS t(id, tags)
```

Return six columns in this order, ordered by `id` ascending (3 rows):

- `id`
- `first_tag` — element 1
- `zeroth` — element 0
- `tail` — the slice from element 2 to element 3
- `len` — `array_length(tags, 1)`
- `card` — `cardinality(tags)`

Row 1 gives `eco`, NULL, `{limited,recycled}`, 3, 3. Row 2 gives `sale`,
NULL, `{}`, 1, 1. Row 3 gives NULL, NULL, `{}`, **NULL**, **0** — and that
last pair is the reason this exercise exists.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Subscripting uses square brackets, and a slice is two subscripts separated
by a colon. Nothing in an array subscript ever raises an error, which is
the point being made.

## Hint 2

The syntax, all in one place:

```sql
SELECT a[1] AS first, a[2:3] AS slice
FROM (SELECT ARRAY[10,20,30] AS a) s;
```

## Hint 3

Six columns, no functions beyond the two measuring ones. The only thing to
be careful about is that `array_length` needs a second argument naming the
dimension — a bare `array_length(tags)` does not exist.

Take a moment on row 3 before you move on: one of the two measurements
returns NULL on an empty array and the other returns zero, and every
`WHERE` clause you write about "arrays with elements" depends on which one
you picked.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the storage layout. An array header records dimensions and their
lower bounds, and the lower bound of an array you build with `ARRAY[...]` is
1. So `tags[0]` is not "the first element" and it is not an error either —
it is a request for a position outside the stored range, and out-of-range
reads return NULL by design.

## Hint 2

That same design explains the empty-array case. An empty array has *zero
dimensions*, not one dimension of length zero. Ask `array_length` about
dimension 1 of a zero-dimensional array and the honest answer is "there is
no such dimension" — which is NULL. `cardinality` counts elements
regardless of dimensions and answers 0.

## Hint 3

The practical rule that falls out: write emptiness tests as
`cardinality(a) = 0`, never as `array_length(a, 1) = 0`, which is a
condition that can never be true and which will therefore never appear in
your test failures.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex1 — indexing, slicing, measuring
SELECT id,
       tags[1]              AS first_tag,
       tags[0]              AS zeroth,
       tags[2:3]            AS tail,
       array_length(tags, 1) AS len,
       cardinality(tags)     AS card
FROM (VALUES (1, ARRAY['eco', 'limited', 'recycled']),
             (2, ARRAY['sale']),
             (3, ARRAY[]::text[])) AS t(id, tags)
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex1 — the same facts via the bound functions
SELECT id,
       tags[array_lower(tags, 1)]                       AS first_tag,
       tags[0]                                          AS zeroth,
       tags[2:3]                                        AS tail,
       array_upper(tags, 1) - array_lower(tags, 1) + 1   AS len,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM unnest(tags))::int          AS card
FROM (VALUES (1, ARRAY['eco', 'limited', 'recycled']),
             (2, ARRAY['sale']),
             (3, ARRAY[]::text[])) AS t(id, tags)
ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — collect rows into an array

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. For the twenty products with `id <= 20`, collect
their names per category.

Return three columns in this order:

- `category`
- `names` — a `text[]` of the product names in that category, **ordered by
  product id ascending**
- `n` — how many names are in the array

**Ordered by `category` ascending.** One row per category that appears
among those twenty products.

The element order inside `names` is part of the answer. An aggregate
without an explicit order produces whatever the executor delivered, which
is a property of the plan and not of your query.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`array_agg` is an ordinary aggregate: it goes in the select list, it works
with `GROUP BY`, and it accepts an `ORDER BY` clause of its own inside the
parentheses.

## Hint 2

The syntax for ordering inside an aggregate call:

```sql
SELECT string_agg(name, ',' ORDER BY id) FROM products WHERE id <= 5;
```

`array_agg` takes the same clause in the same position.

## Hint 3

Group by category, aggregate the names with the ordering inside the call,
and count. For the count you can use `count(*)` or measure the array you
just built — pick one and be able to say why the other would also be
correct here but not always.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what would break without the ordering. Today the plan is probably a
sequential scan in physical order, which happens to be id order after a
fresh load, so the array looks sorted. Add an index that changes the scan,
or vacuum the table, and the same query returns the same rows with a
different array. That is a bug that appears months later and cannot be
reproduced from the query text.

## Hint 2

The general rule this exercise is teaching: an aggregate that produces an
*ordered container* must say what the order is. That covers `array_agg`,
`string_agg`, `jsonb_agg` and `xmlagg`. Aggregates that produce unordered
values — `sum`, `count`, `bool_and` — need no such clause and accept none
usefully.

## Hint 3

If you use `cardinality(array_agg(...))` for the count, note you cannot
nest one aggregate inside another. You would need the array in a subquery
first. `count(*)` in the same select list is the simpler answer, and
knowing why the other route needs a subquery is worth the detour.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex2 — collect rows into an array
SELECT category,
       array_agg(name ORDER BY id) AS names,
       count(*)                    AS n
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex2 — array constructed from a correlated subquery
SELECT c.category,
       ARRAY(SELECT p.name
             FROM products p
             WHERE p.id <= 20 AND p.category = c.category
             ORDER BY p.id) AS names,
       (SELECT count(*)
        FROM products p
        WHERE p.id <= 20 AND p.category = c.category)::bigint AS n
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products WHERE id <= 20) c
ORDER BY c.category;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — split, then unnest with position

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Customer emails have the shape
`something@domain.tld`.

For the five customers with `id <= 5`, split the email on `@` and return
one row per part: three columns in this order, `id`, `pos`, `part`.

- `pos` is the one-based position of the part, as produced by
  `WITH ORDINALITY`
- `part` is the text of that part

**Ordered by `id` ascending, then `pos` ascending.** (10 rows — every email
has exactly two parts.)

So customer 1 yields two rows: `1 | 1 | <local part>` and
`1 | 2 | <domain>`.

Use `string_to_array` and `unnest ... WITH ORDINALITY`. Doing it with
`split_part` twice and a `UNION ALL` produces the same rows and misses the
point.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two steps: text becomes an array, then the array becomes rows. The second
step goes in the `FROM` clause, beside the table, where it can see the
table's columns.

## Hint 2

The `WITH ORDINALITY` shape looks like this:

```sql
SELECT t.word, t.n
FROM unnest(string_to_array('a b c', ' ')) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(word, n);
```

Note the alias carries *two* names: one for the value, one for the
position.

## Hint 3

Put the customers table and the function side by side in `FROM`, separated
by a comma, and let the function reference `email`. The ordering clause
then names both the customer id and the position column — and remember the
position is a `bigint`, which matters only if you compare it to something
typed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from what ordinality is *for*. `unnest` returns rows in array
order, and if you select them straight out you will see them in that order
— but nothing in the SQL model guarantees it survives a join, a
`DISTINCT`, or a parallel plan. Ordinality captures the position as data,
at the moment it is still known.

## Hint 2

That makes it the tool for any "keep the sequence" problem: reconstructing
a document's paragraphs in order, matching a CSV header row to its values,
recovering which of a customer's addresses was first. Splitting an email is
the smallest possible version of that problem.

## Hint 3

A detail that trips people: `WITH ORDINALITY` attaches to the function
call, not to the alias, and the alias then has to name both output columns.
If PostgreSQL complains that the table `t` has 1 column available but 2
specified, you have written the ordinality clause in the wrong place.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex3 — split, then unnest with position
SELECT c.id,
       e.pos,
       e.part
FROM customers c,
     unnest(string_to_array(c.email, '@')) WITH ORDINALITY AS e(part, pos)
WHERE c.id <= 5
ORDER BY c.id, e.pos;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex3 — positions generated against the array
SELECT c.id,
       g.pos,
       (string_to_array(c.email, '@'))[g.pos] AS part
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(
       1, cardinality(string_to_array(c.email, '@'))) AS g(pos)
WHERE c.id <= 5
ORDER BY c.id, g.pos;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the set operators

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Each product's JSONB `attributes` carries a
two-element `tags` array. Derive it as a `text[]` and ask three different
set questions of it.

For the products with `id <= 200`, return five columns in this order:

- `id`
- `tags` — the tags as a `text[]`
- `has_eco` — boolean, does the tag array contain `eco`
- `overlaps_sale` — boolean, does it share any element with
  `ARRAY['eco','sale']`
- `subset_pair` — boolean, is it contained by `ARRAY['eco','limited']`

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (200 rows.)

The three booleans use three different operators, and no two of them are
the same question. Be able to name a product for which `has_eco` is true
and `subset_pair` is false before you run it.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Getting from a JSONB array to a `text[]` is a job for an array constructor
around a set-returning function, or for a dedicated conversion function
that exists for exactly this.

## Hint 2

Two ways to build the array:

```sql
SELECT ARRAY(SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text('["a","b"]'::jsonb));
SELECT array_agg(x) FROM jsonb_array_elements_text('["a","b"]'::jsonb) AS t(x);
```

The first is a scalar expression you can put straight in a select list.

## Hint 3

Build the array once in a CTE or a subquery and ask the three questions of
the result — repeating the construction three times works and is exactly
the sort of thing that makes a query four times slower than it needs to be.
The three operators are containment, overlap and contained-by; deciding
which symbol is which is the part left to you.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look at where the cost is. The array is *derived*, so every row scanned
allocates a new array before any predicate can use it. That is fine on two
hundred rows and ruinous on three million, and no index can help because
there is no stored value to index.

## Hint 2

Which tells you what the production shape of this query is. Either the tags
live in a real `text[]` column with a GIN index on it, or the predicate is
expressed against the JSONB directly with `@>` so that lesson 42's index
applies. Deriving an array in order to use array operators is a debugging
convenience, not a plan.

## Hint 3

Worth doing in the lab afterwards: build an expression index on
`(ARRAY(SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags')))` and watch
PostgreSQL refuse it, because the expression is not immutable in the way an
index requires. That refusal is the system telling you the same thing this
hint is.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex4 — the set operators
WITH t AS (
  SELECT id,
         ARRAY(SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags'))
           AS tags
  FROM products
  WHERE id <= 200
)
SELECT id,
       tags,
       tags @> ARRAY['eco']               AS has_eco,
       tags && ARRAY['eco', 'sale']       AS overlaps_sale,
       tags <@ ARRAY['eco', 'limited']    AS subset_pair
FROM t
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex4 — the same questions asked of the JSONB directly
SELECT p.id,
       array_agg(e.tag ORDER BY e.ord)                       AS tags,
       bool_or(e.tag = 'eco')                                AS has_eco,
       bool_or(e.tag IN ('eco', 'sale'))                     AS overlaps_sale,
       bool_and(e.tag IN ('eco', 'limited'))                 AS subset_pair
FROM products p,
     jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags')
       WITH ORDINALITY AS e(tag, ord)
WHERE p.id <= 200
GROUP BY p.id
ORDER BY p.id;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — ANY, ALL and IN

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Three quantified comparisons over the same list.

Return one row with four columns, in this order:

- `by_in` — how many products have `id IN (7, 42, 100, 999999)`
- `by_any` — the same count written with `= ANY` and an array literal
- `above_all` — how many products have a price greater than **every** value
  in `ARRAY[10, 25, 60]::numeric[]`
- `empty_any` — how many products satisfy `id = ANY (ARRAY[]::int[])`

`by_in` and `by_any` agree — that is the point of the pair. `above_all` is
just `price > 60` written the other way round. `empty_any` is 0, and the
reason it is 0 rather than a syntax error is the reason `= ANY` is what you
parameterise with.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`x = ANY (arr)` is true when `x` equals at least one element. `x > ALL
(arr)` is true when `x` beats every element. Both take an array on the
right, in parentheses.

## Hint 2

The form to copy:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE category = ANY (ARRAY['garden','office']);
```

## Hint 3

Four filtered counts over one scan. Watch the types on `above_all`: the
price column is `numeric` and an untyped `ARRAY[10, 25, 60]` will be
inferred as `integer[]`, so either cast the array or let the comparison
resolve — try it both ways and read what PostgreSQL says.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason to prefer `= ANY` has nothing to do with speed; the planner
turns both into the same thing for a literal list. It is about the
*interface*. `IN (...)` needs as many bind parameters as there are values,
so an application that filters by a list of ids either builds SQL by string
concatenation — the classic injection surface — or generates a different
prepared statement for every list length, defeating the plan cache.

## Hint 2

`= ANY ($1)` takes one parameter of array type, whatever the list length.
One statement, one plan, no string building. That is why every mature
driver exposes array binding, and why this idiom is worth adopting even in
queries you write by hand.

## Hint 3

The empty case seals it: `IN ()` does not parse, so the application needs a
special path when the list is empty, and that special path is where the bug
lives. `= ANY (ARRAY[]::int[])` is simply false for every row. Note the
cast — an empty array literal has no element type until you give it one.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex5 — ANY, ALL and IN
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE id IN (7, 42, 100, 999999))          AS by_in,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE id = ANY (ARRAY[7, 42, 100, 999999])) AS by_any,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE price > ALL (ARRAY[10, 25, 60]::numeric[]))
         AS above_all,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE id = ANY (ARRAY[]::int[]))            AS empty_any
FROM products;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex5 — the same four counts as scalar subqueries
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE id IN (7, 42, 100, 999999))
         AS by_in,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM products
        WHERE id = ANY (ARRAY[7, 42, 100, 999999])) AS by_any,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM products
        WHERE price > (SELECT max(v) FROM unnest(ARRAY[10, 25, 60]::numeric[])
                                          AS u(v))) AS above_all,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM products
        WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM unnest(ARRAY[]::int[]) AS u(v)
                      WHERE u.v = products.id)) AS empty_any;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — two arrays, side by side

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. `unnest` takes more than one array and expands
them in lockstep.

Work from this exact input, inline:

```sql
(VALUES (1, ARRAY['a','b','c'], ARRAY[10, 20, 30]),
        (2, ARRAY['x','y'],     ARRAY[1, 2, 3, 4])) AS t(id, labels, weights)
```

Return four columns in this order — `id`, `pos`, `label`, `weight` — with
one row per expanded position, **ordered by `id` ascending then `pos`
ascending**. (7 rows: three for id 1, four for id 2.)

Row set for id 2 ends with `2 | 3 | NULL | 3` and `2 | 4 | NULL | 4`: the
shorter array is padded with NULLs rather than truncating the longer one or
raising. That silent padding is the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The multi-argument form of `unnest` is written with both arrays in one
call, and it is only legal in the `FROM` clause. The alias then names one
column per argument.

## Hint 2

Shape:

```sql
SELECT * FROM unnest(ARRAY[1,2], ARRAY['a','b']) AS u(n, s);
```

## Hint 3

Add `WITH ORDINALITY` for the position column, which means the alias now
names three columns: two values and the ordinal. If PostgreSQL complains
about the number of columns in the alias, count them again — the ordinal is
the last one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why this exists at all. Two `unnest` calls in the same `FROM` clause
separated by a comma would produce a *cross join*: three labels times four
weights is twelve rows, not four. The multi-argument form is the only
built-in way to zip rather than multiply.

## Hint 2

Which means the padding rule is a deliberate choice with a consequence. If
your two arrays are supposed to be parallel — names and values from a form
submission, say — a length mismatch is a data error, and this function
turns it into NULLs that flow downstream. Nothing warns you.

## Hint 3

So the production version of this pattern carries its own check: compare
`cardinality` of the two arrays before expanding, and raise or route the
row elsewhere when they disagree. Write the expansion for the gate, then
write the check you would add in real code and convince yourself where it
belongs.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex6 — two arrays, side by side
SELECT t.id,
       u.pos,
       u.label,
       u.weight
FROM (VALUES (1, ARRAY['a','b','c'], ARRAY[10, 20, 30]),
             (2, ARRAY['x','y'],     ARRAY[1, 2, 3, 4])) AS t(id, labels, weights),
     unnest(t.labels, t.weights) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(label, weight, pos)
ORDER BY t.id, u.pos;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex6 — zipped by generated position instead
SELECT t.id,
       g.pos,
       t.labels[g.pos]  AS label,
       t.weights[g.pos] AS weight
FROM (VALUES (1, ARRAY['a','b','c'], ARRAY[10, 20, 30]),
             (2, ARRAY['x','y'],     ARRAY[1, 2, 3, 4])) AS t(id, labels, weights)
CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(
       1, greatest(cardinality(t.labels), cardinality(t.weights))) AS g(pos)
ORDER BY t.id, g.pos;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — NULLs inside arrays

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. An array can contain NULL, and every operator has
an opinion about it.

Work from this exact input, inline:

```sql
(VALUES (1, ARRAY['eco', 'limited']),
        (2, ARRAY['eco', NULL]),
        (3, ARRAY[NULL, NULL]::text[])) AS t(id, tags)
```

Return five columns in this order, ordered by `id` ascending (3 rows):

- `id`
- `card` — `cardinality(tags)`
- `pos_of_limited` — `array_position(tags, 'limited')`
- `without_nulls` — `array_remove(tags, NULL)`
- `sale_matches` — the result of `'sale' = ANY (tags)`

Row 1: 2, 2, `{eco,limited}`, false. Row 2: 2, NULL, `{eco}`, **NULL**.
Row 3: 2, NULL, `{}`, **NULL**.

The last column is the one to think about. `'sale'` is not in any of these
arrays, yet two rows answer NULL rather than false, because an unknown
element makes "no match anywhere" unprovable.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four functions and one quantified comparison, applied to the same column.
None of them needs a subquery.

## Hint 2

`array_remove` takes the array and the value to strip, and it accepts NULL
as that value:

```sql
SELECT array_remove(ARRAY[1, NULL, 2], NULL);   -- {1,2}
```

## Hint 3

Write the five columns straight out. The only surprise is the last one, and
it is not a surprise you can code around here — just let the NULL through
and make sure your column is typed boolean, not text.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from lesson 05's three-valued logic and apply it element by element.
`'sale' = ANY (ARRAY['eco', NULL])` expands to `'sale' = 'eco' OR 'sale' =
NULL`, which is `false OR NULL`, which is NULL. If any comparison had been
true, the whole thing would be true — `true OR NULL` is true — which is why
a NULL element does not poison a positive match, only a negative one.

## Hint 2

That asymmetry is what makes NULLs in arrays genuinely dangerous. A filter
written `WHERE NOT ('sale' = ANY (tags))` drops rows 2 and 3 silently,
because `NOT NULL` is NULL and a NULL predicate is not true. The rows you
lose are exactly the rows with incomplete data — the ones you most wanted
to find.

## Hint 3

The defences, in order of preference: do not allow NULL elements in the
first place (a `CHECK (array_position(tags, NULL) IS NULL)` constraint says
so declaratively); strip them at read time with `array_remove`; or write
the negative test as `coalesce(NOT ('sale' = ANY (tags)), true)` and be
explicit about which way you want the unknowns to fall.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex7 — NULLs inside arrays
SELECT id,
       cardinality(tags)                AS card,
       array_position(tags, 'limited')  AS pos_of_limited,
       array_remove(tags, NULL)         AS without_nulls,
       'sale' = ANY (tags)              AS sale_matches
FROM (VALUES (1, ARRAY['eco', 'limited']),
             (2, ARRAY['eco', NULL]),
             (3, ARRAY[NULL, NULL]::text[])) AS t(id, tags)
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex7 — the same answers computed by expansion
SELECT t.id,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM unnest(t.tags))::int AS card,
       (SELECT min(u.ord)
        FROM unnest(t.tags) WITH ORDINALITY AS u(tag, ord)
        WHERE u.tag = 'limited')::int             AS pos_of_limited,
       ARRAY(SELECT u.tag FROM unnest(t.tags) AS u(tag)
             WHERE u.tag IS NOT NULL)             AS without_nulls,
       (SELECT CASE WHEN bool_or(u.tag = 'sale') THEN true
                    WHEN bool_and(u.tag IS NOT NULL) THEN false
               END
        FROM unnest(t.tags) AS u(tag))            AS sale_matches
FROM (VALUES (1, ARRAY['eco', 'limited']),
             (2, ARRAY['eco', NULL]),
             (3, ARRAY[NULL, NULL]::text[])) AS t(id, tags)
ORDER BY t.id;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the tag matrix

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Describe the tag vocabulary, per category, for the
whole catalogue.

Return four columns in this order:

- `category`
- `tags` — the **distinct** tags used by products in that category, as a
  `text[]` sorted alphabetically
- `n_tags` — how many distinct tags that is
- `top_tag` — the single tag used by the most products in that category;
  break ties by choosing the alphabetically first

**Ordered by `category` ascending.** One row per category.

`tags` and `top_tag` need different shapes of work: one is a distinct
aggregate, the other is a per-category ranking. Doing both in one pass is
the exercise.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start by producing one row per product-tag pair. Everything else is
aggregation over that.

## Hint 2

Once you have pairs, two different groupings are needed: one by category,
one by category and tag. Compute the finer grouping first and aggregate it
again:

```sql
WITH pairs AS (...),
     per_tag AS (SELECT category, tag, count(*) AS uses
                 FROM pairs GROUP BY category, tag)
SELECT category, array_agg(tag ORDER BY tag) FROM per_tag GROUP BY category;
```

## Hint 3

For `top_tag`, you already have the per-category-per-tag counts, so this is
a top-one-per-group problem — lesson 49's `DISTINCT ON`, or a window
function's `row_number`, or an ordered aggregate that takes the first
element. Pick one and make sure the tie-break is in the ordering.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that the distinct aggregate hides a decision. `array_agg(DISTINCT
tag ORDER BY tag)` deduplicates *after* grouping, so it answers "which tags
appear" and loses "how often". That is why the second grouping level exists
in the hint above: you need the counts anyway for `top_tag`, and once you
have them the distinct list is free.

## Hint 2

Then think about what this report tells you. A category whose `n_tags`
equals the whole vocabulary has tags that carry no information about it. A
category with two tags used by everything has an attribute that should have
been a column. Reports like this are how you find out that a flexible
schema has quietly become a rigid one.

## Hint 3

One syntax detail worth knowing before it bites: `array_agg(DISTINCT tag
ORDER BY uses DESC)` is rejected, because when `DISTINCT` is present the
sort expression must be the same expression being deduplicated. That
restriction is why the ranking has to happen outside the aggregate rather
than inside it.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex8 — the tag matrix
WITH pairs AS (
  SELECT p.category, e.tag
  FROM products p,
       jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS e(tag)
), per_tag AS (
  SELECT category, tag, count(*) AS uses
  FROM pairs
  GROUP BY category, tag
), ranked AS (
  SELECT category, tag,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category
                            ORDER BY uses DESC, tag) AS rn
  FROM per_tag
)
SELECT pt.category,
       array_agg(pt.tag ORDER BY pt.tag) AS tags,
       count(*)                          AS n_tags,
       max(r.tag) FILTER (WHERE r.rn = 1) AS top_tag
FROM per_tag pt
JOIN ranked r ON r.category = pt.category AND r.tag = pt.tag
GROUP BY pt.category
ORDER BY pt.category;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / ex8 — distinct aggregate plus a DISTINCT ON lookup
WITH pairs AS (
  SELECT p.category, e.tag
  FROM products p,
       jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS e(tag)
), per_tag AS (
  SELECT category, tag, count(*) AS uses
  FROM pairs
  GROUP BY category, tag
), best AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) category, tag
  FROM per_tag
  ORDER BY category, uses DESC, tag
)
SELECT p.category,
       array_agg(DISTINCT p.tag ORDER BY p.tag) AS tags,
       count(DISTINCT p.tag)                    AS n_tags,
       b.tag                                    AS top_tag
FROM pairs p
JOIN best b ON b.category = p.category
GROUP BY p.category, b.tag
ORDER BY p.category;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — products that share a tag set

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Build the "related products" list that a
catalogue page would show.

For each product with `id <= 20`, find the other products (from the whole
catalogue) whose tag set **overlaps** its own, and report the closest five.

Return four columns in this order:

- `id`
- `tags` — the product's own tags as an alphabetically sorted `text[]`
- `neighbours` — a `text[]` of the ids of the five closest other products,
  as text, in the order described below
- `best_overlap` — the number of shared tags with the closest neighbour

"Closest" means: more shared tags first, then lower id. Only products
sharing at least one tag qualify; if fewer than five qualify, return as
many as there are.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Every product carries exactly two tags, so `best_overlap` is 1 or 2.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is a per-row top-five, which means a lateral subquery: for each of the
twenty products, run a small query against the catalogue that already knows
which product it is working for.

## Hint 2

The overlap count between two arrays is the cardinality of their
intersection, and there is no intersection operator for arrays — but there
is one obvious way to compute it from `unnest` and one from `= ANY`:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM unnest(a) AS u(x) WHERE u.x = ANY (b);
```

## Hint 3

Structure: derive the tag array per product in a CTE; then, for each of the
twenty, a lateral that filters the catalogue with `&&` (cheap, prunes most
rows), computes the overlap count for the survivors, orders by that count
descending then id, and limits to five. The outer query then aggregates the
neighbour ids into an array — with an `ORDER BY` that matches the lateral's,
because an aggregate does not inherit a subquery's ordering.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about the pruning. Without the `&&` filter, each of the twenty
laterals computes an overlap count against ten thousand products: two
hundred thousand array intersections. With it, the filter rejects
non-overlapping products with one operator before any counting happens.
That is the same principle as a partial index — cheap test first, expensive
test on the survivors.

## Hint 2

Then consider whether even that is enough at real scale. On a catalogue of
ten million, the right answer is a stored `text[]` column with a GIN index,
so `&&` becomes an index scan instead of a filter. Everything in this query
stays the same; only the source of the array changes. Write it so that
swapping the CTE for a real column is a one-line edit.

## Hint 3

Two details that decide correctness. The product must not be its own
neighbour, so the lateral needs an inequality on id. And `array_agg` over
the lateral's rows does not preserve the lateral's `ORDER BY` — put the
ordering inside the aggregate call, ordering by the same two expressions,
or your neighbour list will be right in content and wrong in order.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / challenge — products that share a tag set
WITH tagged AS (
  SELECT id,
         ARRAY(SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags')) AS tags
  FROM products
)
SELECT t.id,
       ARRAY(SELECT x FROM unnest(t.tags) AS u(x) ORDER BY x) AS tags,
       coalesce(n.neighbours, ARRAY[]::text[])                AS neighbours,
       n.best_overlap
FROM tagged t
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT array_agg(c.id::text ORDER BY c.shared DESC, c.id) AS neighbours,
         max(c.shared)                                      AS best_overlap
  FROM (
    SELECT o.id,
           (SELECT count(*) FROM unnest(t.tags) AS u(x)
            WHERE u.x = ANY (o.tags)) AS shared
    FROM tagged o
    WHERE o.id <> t.id
      AND o.tags && t.tags
    ORDER BY shared DESC, o.id
    LIMIT 5
  ) c
) n ON true
WHERE t.id <= 20
ORDER BY t.id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / challenge — overlap computed by intersecting rows
WITH tagged AS (
  SELECT id,
         ARRAY(SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags')) AS tags
  FROM products
), seeds AS (
  SELECT id, tags FROM tagged WHERE id <= 20
), overlaps AS (
  SELECT s.id AS seed_id,
         o.id AS other_id,
         cardinality(ARRAY(SELECT x FROM unnest(s.tags) AS u(x)
                           INTERSECT
                           SELECT y FROM unnest(o.tags) AS v(y))) AS shared
  FROM seeds s
  JOIN tagged o ON o.id <> s.id AND o.tags && s.tags
), ranked AS (
  SELECT seed_id, other_id, shared,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY seed_id
                            ORDER BY shared DESC, other_id) AS rn
  FROM overlaps
)
SELECT s.id,
       ARRAY(SELECT x FROM unnest(s.tags) AS u(x) ORDER BY x) AS tags,
       coalesce((SELECT array_agg(r.other_id::text ORDER BY r.rn)
                 FROM ranked r
                 WHERE r.seed_id = s.id AND r.rn <= 5), ARRAY[]::text[])
         AS neighbours,
       (SELECT max(r.shared) FROM ranked r
        WHERE r.seed_id = s.id AND r.rn = 1) AS best_overlap
FROM seeds s
ORDER BY s.id;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the array column, and its price

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Build the array-column design properly, then
show what it cannot do.

Write a script that:

1. Creates a table `catalogue` with `id int primary key`, `name text not
   null`, and `tags text[] not null default '{}'`.
2. Creates a **GIN index** on `tags`.
3. Inserts four rows:
   - `(1, 'watering can', '{garden,eco}')`
   - `(2, 'desk lamp', '{office,eco}')`
   - `(3, 'compost bin', '{garden,recycled}')`
   - `(4, 'blank slate', '{}')`
4. Finishes with a `SELECT` returning, for every row, four columns in this
   order — `id`, `name`, `is_eco`, `n_tags` — where `is_eco` is a
   containment test against `ARRAY['eco']` and `n_tags` is the element
   count, **ordered by `id` ascending** (4 rows).

Row 4 must report `false` and `0`, which is the empty-array behaviour from
exercise 1 arriving in a real schema.

Then answer this in a trailing SQL comment, in one or two lines: name the
two things this design cannot do that a `catalogue_tags` junction table
with a foreign key could. The gate does not read your comment; the next
engineer does.

```
uv run dojo test v3c03_arrays_unnest review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three statements and a query. The array literal form in an `INSERT` is the
brace-and-quote form, `'{garden,eco}'`, which is often easier to read in
bulk data than `ARRAY['garden','eco']`.

## Hint 2

The index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX catalogue_tags_idx ON catalogue USING gin (tags);
```

The default operator class for arrays supports `@>`, `<@`, `&&` and `=`.

## Hint 3

For the final query, use the containment operator rather than
`'eco' = ANY (tags)`. Both are correct; only one of them is a predicate the
GIN index you just built can serve, and on four rows the planner will
ignore both — which is itself worth confirming with `EXPLAIN`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The two missing capabilities are worth naming precisely, because "no
integrity" is too vague to argue with. First: nothing prevents
`'{gardn}'`. There is no reference to a tag table, so a typo is a new tag,
silently, forever, and no constraint in the database can notice. Second:
the relationship can carry no data. You cannot record when a tag was
applied, by whom, or with what confidence, because there is no row to hang
those columns on.

## Hint 2

A third, subtler one you can mention for credit: the planner has no
statistics about individual array elements beyond the most-common-elements
list it keeps for array columns, so selectivity estimates for `@>` on a
rare tag versus a ubiquitous one are cruder than they would be for a
junction table's indexed column. Cruder estimates mean worse join orders in
big queries.

## Hint 3

And the honest counterweight, which belongs in your comment too: with the
GIN index in place, the *query* performance argument favours the array. One
index scan and no join beats a join to a junction table for pure "find rows
with this tag" work. The junction table wins on integrity and
extensibility, not on speed, and a design note that pretends otherwise will
not survive its first review.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / review1 — the array column, and its price
CREATE TABLE catalogue (
  id   int   PRIMARY KEY,
  name text  NOT NULL,
  tags text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

CREATE INDEX catalogue_tags_idx ON catalogue USING gin (tags);

INSERT INTO catalogue (id, name, tags) VALUES
  (1, 'watering can', '{garden,eco}'),
  (2, 'desk lamp',    '{office,eco}'),
  (3, 'compost bin',  '{garden,recycled}'),
  (4, 'blank slate',  '{}');

SELECT id,
       name,
       tags @> ARRAY['eco'] AS is_eco,
       cardinality(tags)    AS n_tags
FROM catalogue
ORDER BY id;

-- No foreign key can reference an array element, so a misspelt tag is
-- indistinguishable from a new one; and the relationship itself can carry
-- no columns (applied_at, applied_by) because it has no row to live in.
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c03_arrays_unnest / review1 — same schema, membership asked another way
CREATE TABLE catalogue (
  id   int    PRIMARY KEY,
  name text   NOT NULL,
  tags text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);

CREATE INDEX catalogue_tags_idx ON catalogue USING gin (tags);

INSERT INTO catalogue (id, name, tags) VALUES
  (1, 'watering can', ARRAY['garden','eco']),
  (2, 'desk lamp',    ARRAY['office','eco']),
  (3, 'compost bin',  ARRAY['garden','recycled']),
  (4, 'blank slate',  ARRAY[]::text[]);

SELECT id,
       name,
       coalesce('eco' = ANY (tags), false)         AS is_eco,
       coalesce(array_length(tags, 1), 0)          AS n_tags
FROM catalogue
ORDER BY id;

lessons.title: V3·C4 — Full-text search: tsvector, ranking, dictionaries
lessons.summary: Lesson 41 built a GIN index over to_tsvector and searched a million reviews. This sector is about everything that index was hiding: what a dictionary chain does to a word, which of the four query parsers to expose to users, how ranking is actually computed, and why the configuration name is part of your schema.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·C4 — Full-text search: tsvector, ranking, dictionaries

Lesson 41 gave you a working search: `to_tsvector('english', body) @@
to_tsquery('english', 'excellent & battery')`, a GIN index over the
expression, and a large speedup. It also left every interesting decision
unmade. Which parser should a search box use? Why did `excellent` match
`excellently`, and what else did it match that you did not intend? What is
`ts_rank` actually ranking, and why does a long document score lower? And
what happens to that index the day someone changes a session setting?

This sector answers those. The mechanism is smaller than it looks: a
configuration is a mapping from token types to dictionary chains, a
dictionary is a function from a word to a lexeme or nothing, and everything
else — stemming, stopwords, unaccenting, synonyms — is a dictionary doing
its job.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The batteries were excellent, and running.');
-- 'batteri':2 'excel':4 'run':6
```

Three things happened. The parser split the string into tokens and gave
each a type (word, numword, email, url, and about twenty more). Each token
went through the dictionary chain configured for its type: `the` and `were`
and `and` were dropped as stopwords, `batteries` was stemmed to `batteri`,
`excellent` to `excel`, `running` to `run`. And the surviving lexemes were
stored, sorted and deduplicated, each with its position in the original
text.

Positions are why phrase search works, and weights are how you say some
text matters more:

```sql
SELECT setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'Cordless drill'), 'A') ||
       setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'A drill for wood'), 'B');
-- 'cordless':1A 'drill':2A,4B 'wood':6B
```

Four query builders, and choosing between them is a security-adjacent
decision:

```sql
to_tsquery('english', 'battery & !dead')     -- operators; RAISES on junk
plainto_tsquery('english', 'dead battery')   -- ANDs the words together
phraseto_tsquery('english', 'battery life')  -- 'batteri' <-> 'life'
websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')  -- Google-ish
```

`to_tsquery` is for developers: it accepts `&`, `|`, `!`, `<->`, `<N>` and
parentheses, and it raises a syntax error on anything else — so it must
never see raw user input. `websearch_to_tsquery` is the one to put behind a
search box: quoted phrases, `or`, and leading `-` for negation, and it
never raises.

Ranking is a separate step from matching:

```sql
ORDER BY ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body),
                 websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery'), 32) DESC
```

`ts_rank` scores by how often the query terms occur and with what weights.
`ts_rank_cd` scores by *cover density* — how close the terms are to each
other — and needs positions, so it cannot be used on a stripped vector. The
last argument is a normalisation bitmask, and its most useful bits divide
the score by document length so that a long review does not win on volume
alone.

Finally, the trap that outlives every other detail here:

```sql
-- indexable, immutable, correct
CREATE INDEX ON reviews USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body));
-- NOT indexable: depends on default_text_search_config
CREATE INDEX ON reviews USING gin (to_tsvector(body));
```

The one-argument form reads a session setting, which makes it *stable*
rather than *immutable*, and PostgreSQL refuses to index it. The
configuration name is part of your schema. Write it out, every time,
everywhere, and make sure the query spells the same expression the index
does.

The modern way to guarantee that agreement is not discipline, it is a
column:

```sql
ALTER TABLE reviews
  ADD COLUMN tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED;
CREATE INDEX reviews_tsv_idx ON reviews USING gin (tsv);
-- every query now says: WHERE tsv @@ <query>
```

One expression, written once, in the table definition. The index cannot
drift from the query because there is nothing left to drift. The price is
storage and per-write computation, which on a read-heavy corpus is the
right side of the trade.

One diagnostic is worth learning now, because it answers most "why did that
not match" questions in a single query: `ts_debug('english', 'some text')`
returns one row per token showing its type, the dictionaries that were
tried, and the lexemes that came out. When stemming or a stopword surprises
you, that function tells you which part of the pipeline did it.

## Exercise 1 — what the dictionary did

Read the lexemes out of a sentence and count them, and see stopwords and
stemming happen.

## Exercise 2 — four ways to ask

The same user input through all four query builders, matched against the
same document, with the differences visible in one row.

## Exercise 3 — search the corpus

A real search over a million review bodies, using the builder you would
actually expose to a user.

## Exercise 4 — rank, and normalise

`ts_rank` with and without length normalisation, on the same matches, so
you can see what the bitmask changes.

## Exercise 5 — weights

Combine a product's name and description into one weighted vector and rank
with a custom weight array.

## Exercise 6 — phrases and distance

`phraseto_tsquery`, the `<->` operator, and the `<N>` form that allows a
gap.

## Exercise 7 — two configurations

`simple` versus `english` on the same text. One stems and drops stopwords;
the other does neither, and there are searches for which that is the right
answer.

## Exercise 8 — the snippet

`ts_headline` produces the highlighted extract a result list shows. It is
also the most expensive part of a search page, and you will see why.

## Challenge — a searchable table

Build the whole thing: a table with a stored generated tsvector column,
weighted across two fields, a GIN index, and a ranked query with snippets.

## Review 1 — the configuration is schema

Demonstrate the immutability rule, then write the index and the query that
agree with each other. This is the failure that silently costs a production
search page its index.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3c04_fulltext

Full-text search in PostgreSQL is a pipeline of small, replaceable parts.
Almost every surprise it produces comes from one of the parts doing exactly
what it was configured to do, to text you had not thought about.

## Notes

**The parser splits, the dictionaries decide.** A text search configuration
is a mapping from *token type* to an ordered list of dictionaries. The
parser assigns each token a type — `asciiword`, `word`, `numword`, `email`,
`url`, `host`, `int`, `float` and others. For each token, the dictionaries
for its type are tried in order: the first one that returns lexemes wins,
one that returns an empty result marks the token a stopword and stops the
chain, and one that returns NULL passes the token to the next dictionary.

**A dictionary is a function, not a word list.** `simple` lowercases and
returns the word. `english_stem` (Snowball) lowercases, drops stopwords from
its list, and stems. `unaccent` strips diacritics and passes the result on,
which is why it is usually configured as a *filtering* dictionary in front
of a stemmer. `synonym` and `thesaurus` map words or phrases to other
words. You can chain them, and the chain is where behaviour lives.

**Stemming is aggressive and lossy.** `excellent`, `excellently` and
`excellence` all become `excel`, and so does `excel`. That is a feature for
recall and a problem for precision, and it is not configurable per query.
If you need exact matching on a term, index a `simple` vector alongside the
`english` one.

**Positions cost, and enable.** `to_tsvector` records the position of each
lexeme, capped at 16383. Positions make phrase search and `ts_rank_cd`
possible. `strip()` removes them, making the vector smaller — and making
both of those impossible. Do not strip a vector you intend to search
phrases in.

**Weights are labels, not numbers.** `setweight` marks lexemes A, B, C or
D, and the numbers are supplied at rank time by a four-element array in the
order `{D, C, B, A}` — a reversal that catches everyone. The default is
`{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0}`.

**`@@` is matching; ranking is a second pass.** The index finds candidate
rows; `ts_rank` then runs over those rows only. That is why ranking is
cheap when the query is selective and expensive when it is not, and why
`ORDER BY rank LIMIT 10` over a term matching half the corpus is a slow
query no index can save.

**Normalisation is a bitmask, and 32 is the friendly one.** Bit 1 divides
by `1 + log(length)`, bit 2 divides by length, bit 8 and 16 do the same
with unique word counts, and bit 32 maps the rank into `rank/(rank+1)`,
giving a bounded 0-to-1 score that is comparable across queries. Combine
with `|`.

**`websearch_to_tsquery` is the only one safe for raw input.**
`to_tsquery` raises on malformed input; `plainto_tsquery` and
`phraseto_tsquery` never raise but ignore user intent, ANDing everything.
`websearch_to_tsquery` understands quotes, `or`, and `-negation`, and
degrades gracefully.

**The configuration name is part of the expression.** An index on
`to_tsvector('english', body)` serves only queries that spell that exact
expression. `to_tsvector('simple', body)`, or the one-argument form, or a
different column, are all different expressions and get no index. This is
the most common cause of "search got slow overnight".

**GIN or GiST, and it is usually GIN.** GIN stores every lexeme as a key
and is exact, large and slower to update. GiST stores a fixed-size
signature per row — a bloom filter of the lexemes — so it is small, cheap
to update, and lossy: it returns false positives that are rechecked against
the heap. Read-mostly corpora want GIN. A queue-like table being rewritten
constantly may want GiST.

**Generated columns are the modern shape.** `tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS
AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED` gives you a real column to index,
to inspect, and to reference in queries — no expression to keep in sync
between index and query, at the cost of storing the vector.

## ex1 — what the dictionary did

# V3·C4 — Full-text search: tsvector, ranking, dictionaries

Lesson 41 gave you a working search: `to_tsvector('english', body) @@
to_tsquery('english', 'excellent & battery')`, a GIN index over the
expression, and a large speedup. It also left every interesting decision
unmade. Which parser should a search box use? Why did `excellent` match
`excellently`, and what else did it match that you did not intend? What is
`ts_rank` actually ranking, and why does a long document score lower? And
what happens to that index the day someone changes a session setting?

This sector answers those. The mechanism is smaller than it looks: a
configuration is a mapping from token types to dictionary chains, a
dictionary is a function from a word to a lexeme or nothing, and everything
else — stemming, stopwords, unaccenting, synonyms — is a dictionary doing
its job.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The batteries were excellent, and running.');
-- 'batteri':2 'excel':4 'run':6
```

Three things happened. The parser split the string into tokens and gave
each a type (word, numword, email, url, and about twenty more). Each token
went through the dictionary chain configured for its type: `the` and `were`
and `and` were dropped as stopwords, `batteries` was stemmed to `batteri`,
`excellent` to `excel`, `running` to `run`. And the surviving lexemes were
stored, sorted and deduplicated, each with its position in the original
text.

Positions are why phrase search works, and weights are how you say some
text matters more:

```sql
SELECT setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'Cordless drill'), 'A') ||
       setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'A drill for wood'), 'B');
-- 'cordless':1A 'drill':2A,4B 'wood':6B
```

Four query builders, and choosing between them is a security-adjacent
decision:

```sql
to_tsquery('english', 'battery & !dead')     -- operators; RAISES on junk
plainto_tsquery('english', 'dead battery')   -- ANDs the words together
phraseto_tsquery('english', 'battery life')  -- 'batteri' <-> 'life'
websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')  -- Google-ish
```

`to_tsquery` is for developers: it accepts `&`, `|`, `!`, `<->`, `<N>` and
parentheses, and it raises a syntax error on anything else — so it must
never see raw user input. `websearch_to_tsquery` is the one to put behind a
search box: quoted phrases, `or`, and leading `-` for negation, and it
never raises.

Ranking is a separate step from matching:

```sql
ORDER BY ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body),
                 websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery'), 32) DESC
```

`ts_rank` scores by how often the query terms occur and with what weights.
`ts_rank_cd` scores by *cover density* — how close the terms are to each
other — and needs positions, so it cannot be used on a stripped vector. The
last argument is a normalisation bitmask, and its most useful bits divide
the score by document length so that a long review does not win on volume
alone.

Finally, the trap that outlives every other detail here:

```sql
-- indexable, immutable, correct
CREATE INDEX ON reviews USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body));
-- NOT indexable: depends on default_text_search_config
CREATE INDEX ON reviews USING gin (to_tsvector(body));
```

The one-argument form reads a session setting, which makes it *stable*
rather than *immutable*, and PostgreSQL refuses to index it. The
configuration name is part of your schema. Write it out, every time,
everywhere, and make sure the query spells the same expression the index
does.

The modern way to guarantee that agreement is not discipline, it is a
column:

```sql
ALTER TABLE reviews
  ADD COLUMN tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED;
CREATE INDEX reviews_tsv_idx ON reviews USING gin (tsv);
-- every query now says: WHERE tsv @@ <query>
```

One expression, written once, in the table definition. The index cannot
drift from the query because there is nothing left to drift. The price is
storage and per-write computation, which on a read-heavy corpus is the
right side of the trade.

One diagnostic is worth learning now, because it answers most "why did that
not match" questions in a single query: `ts_debug('english', 'some text')`
returns one row per token showing its type, the dictionaries that were
tried, and the lexemes that came out. When stemming or a stopword surprises
you, that function tells you which part of the pipeline did it.

## Exercise 1 — what the dictionary did

Read the lexemes out of a sentence and count them, and see stopwords and
stemming happen.

## Exercise 2 — four ways to ask

The same user input through all four query builders, matched against the
same document, with the differences visible in one row.

## Exercise 3 — search the corpus

A real search over a million review bodies, using the builder you would
actually expose to a user.

## Exercise 4 — rank, and normalise

`ts_rank` with and without length normalisation, on the same matches, so
you can see what the bitmask changes.

## Exercise 5 — weights

Combine a product's name and description into one weighted vector and rank
with a custom weight array.

## Exercise 6 — phrases and distance

`phraseto_tsquery`, the `<->` operator, and the `<N>` form that allows a
gap.

## Exercise 7 — two configurations

`simple` versus `english` on the same text. One stems and drops stopwords;
the other does neither, and there are searches for which that is the right
answer.

## Exercise 8 — the snippet

`ts_headline` produces the highlighted extract a result list shows. It is
also the most expensive part of a search page, and you will see why.

## Challenge — a searchable table

Build the whole thing: a table with a stored generated tsvector column,
weighted across two fields, a GIN index, and a ranked query with snippets.

## Review 1 — the configuration is schema

Demonstrate the immutability rule, then write the index and the query that
agree with each other. This is the failure that silently costs a production
search page its index.

## Common mistakes

**Indexing `to_tsvector(body)` with one argument.** It depends on
`default_text_search_config`, so it is not immutable and cannot be indexed.
If you saw it work, you were looking at a different expression.

**Query and index spelling different expressions.** The index knows
`to_tsvector('english', body)`. A query asking `to_tsvector('english',
lower(body))` or `to_tsvector('simple', body)` gets nothing from it, with
no warning — just a sequential scan and a support ticket.

**Passing user input to `to_tsquery`.** A single quote, ampersand or
unbalanced parenthesis raises an error that reaches the user as a 500.
`websearch_to_tsquery` exists precisely to stop this.

**Ranking before limiting.** `ts_rank` over every matching row when you
want ten of them is usually acceptable; `ts_headline` over every matching
row is not. Rank, order, limit, *then* decorate.

**Reversing the weight array.** `ts_rank('{0.1,0.2,0.4,1.0}', ...)` is
`{D,C,B,A}`. Writing it as A-to-D silently inverts your ranking.

**Expecting `ts_rank` to be comparable across queries.** It is not, unless
you normalise with bit 32. Two searches' raw scores mean nothing to each
other.

**Stripping a vector and then searching phrases.** `strip()` discards
positions; `<->` then matches nothing, quietly.

**Assuming stemming is language-neutral.** The `english` configuration
stems `informatik` and `informacion` too — badly. A multilingual corpus
needs a language column and a configuration chosen per row, which means the
index expression must include that column.

## The interview answer

*"How does full-text search in PostgreSQL work, and how would you make it
fast?"*

Documents are normalised into `tsvector` — a sorted list of lexemes with
positions, produced by a parser that tokenises and a dictionary chain that
stems and drops stopwords. Queries are normalised the same way into
`tsquery`. The `@@` operator tests match. A GIN index over the
`to_tsvector('config', column)` expression, or over a stored generated
column holding it, turns matching into an inverted-index lookup. Ranking
with `ts_rank` runs afterwards, over the matched rows only.

The details that mark experience: use `websearch_to_tsquery` for user
input; store the vector as a generated column so the index expression can
never drift from the query; use weights when you search more than one
field; normalise ranks with the `32` bit if you compare across queries; and
know that this is a good in-database search, not a search engine — no
distributed index, no learning to rank, no typo tolerance without the
trigram work in the next sector.

## Check yourself

1. What are the three stages between a text string and a `tsvector`?
2. Why does searching for `excellent` match a review containing
   `excellently`?
3. Which query builder is safe for raw user input, and what do the other
   three do wrong?
4. What does `setweight` do, and in what order does `ts_rank` take its
   weight array?
5. What is the difference between `ts_rank` and `ts_rank_cd`, and what does
   the second require?
6. What does normalisation bit 32 do, and when do you need it?
7. Why can `to_tsvector(body)` not be indexed?
8. What is the effect of `strip()` on a vector, and what does it break?
9. Write the phrase query for "battery life" two different ways.
10. What does `<2>` mean in a tsquery?
11. When is the `simple` configuration the right choice?
12. Why should `ts_headline` be applied after `LIMIT`?
13. What happens to your search when someone sets
    `default_text_search_config` in a session?
14. How would you support two languages in one searchable table?

# Reading - v3c04_fulltext

Full-text search in PostgreSQL is a pipeline of small, replaceable parts.
Almost every surprise it produces comes from one of the parts doing exactly
what it was configured to do, to text you had not thought about.

## Notes

**The parser splits, the dictionaries decide.** A text search configuration
is a mapping from *token type* to an ordered list of dictionaries. The
parser assigns each token a type — `asciiword`, `word`, `numword`, `email`,
`url`, `host`, `int`, `float` and others. For each token, the dictionaries
for its type are tried in order: the first one that returns lexemes wins,
one that returns an empty result marks the token a stopword and stops the
chain, and one that returns NULL passes the token to the next dictionary.

**A dictionary is a function, not a word list.** `simple` lowercases and
returns the word. `english_stem` (Snowball) lowercases, drops stopwords from
its list, and stems. `unaccent` strips diacritics and passes the result on,
which is why it is usually configured as a *filtering* dictionary in front
of a stemmer. `synonym` and `thesaurus` map words or phrases to other
words. You can chain them, and the chain is where behaviour lives.

**Stemming is aggressive and lossy.** `excellent`, `excellently` and
`excellence` all become `excel`, and so does `excel`. That is a feature for
recall and a problem for precision, and it is not configurable per query.
If you need exact matching on a term, index a `simple` vector alongside the
`english` one.

**Positions cost, and enable.** `to_tsvector` records the position of each
lexeme, capped at 16383. Positions make phrase search and `ts_rank_cd`
possible. `strip()` removes them, making the vector smaller — and making
both of those impossible. Do not strip a vector you intend to search
phrases in.

**Weights are labels, not numbers.** `setweight` marks lexemes A, B, C or
D, and the numbers are supplied at rank time by a four-element array in the
order `{D, C, B, A}` — a reversal that catches everyone. The default is
`{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0}`.

**`@@` is matching; ranking is a second pass.** The index finds candidate
rows; `ts_rank` then runs over those rows only. That is why ranking is
cheap when the query is selective and expensive when it is not, and why
`ORDER BY rank LIMIT 10` over a term matching half the corpus is a slow
query no index can save.

**Normalisation is a bitmask, and 32 is the friendly one.** Bit 1 divides
by `1 + log(length)`, bit 2 divides by length, bit 8 and 16 do the same
with unique word counts, and bit 32 maps the rank into `rank/(rank+1)`,
giving a bounded 0-to-1 score that is comparable across queries. Combine
with `|`.

**`websearch_to_tsquery` is the only one safe for raw input.**
`to_tsquery` raises on malformed input; `plainto_tsquery` and
`phraseto_tsquery` never raise but ignore user intent, ANDing everything.
`websearch_to_tsquery` understands quotes, `or`, and `-negation`, and
degrades gracefully.

**The configuration name is part of the expression.** An index on
`to_tsvector('english', body)` serves only queries that spell that exact
expression. `to_tsvector('simple', body)`, or the one-argument form, or a
different column, are all different expressions and get no index. This is
the most common cause of "search got slow overnight".

**GIN or GiST, and it is usually GIN.** GIN stores every lexeme as a key
and is exact, large and slower to update. GiST stores a fixed-size
signature per row — a bloom filter of the lexemes — so it is small, cheap
to update, and lossy: it returns false positives that are rechecked against
the heap. Read-mostly corpora want GIN. A queue-like table being rewritten
constantly may want GiST.

**Generated columns are the modern shape.** `tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS
AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED` gives you a real column to index,
to inspect, and to reference in queries — no expression to keep in sync
between index and query, at the cost of storing the vector.

## ex1 — what the dictionary did

Count the lexemes and read them. The gap between input words and output
lexemes is the dictionary chain's whole contribution.

## ex2 — four ways to ask

Run the same string through all four and look at the query values
themselves, not just the match results.

## ex3 — search the corpus

The GIN index from lesson 41 is what makes this instant. Try it without and
feel the difference once.

## ex4 — rank, and normalise

The unnormalised ranking favours long documents. Whether that is wrong
depends on your corpus, which is why the flag exists rather than a default.

## ex5 — weights

Note the reversed array order in `ts_rank`. Getting it backwards produces a
ranking that looks plausible and is exactly inverted.

## ex6 — phrases and distance

`<->` is `<1>`. Larger numbers allow gaps, which is how you search for "red
wine" and also match "red table wine".

## ex7 — two configurations

The `simple` configuration is not a toy. Product codes, usernames and tags
should not be stemmed, and searching them with `english` finds things
nobody asked for.

## ex8 — the snippet

`ts_headline` re-parses the *original document* for every row it decorates.
Apply it after the limit, never before.

## Further reading

- [Text Search Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-textsearch.html)
  — `tsvector` and `tsquery`, positions and weights.
- [Controlling Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-controls.html)
  — the four query builders, `ts_rank`, normalisation, and `ts_headline`.
- [Dictionaries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-dictionaries.html)
  — how chains resolve, and how to build a `synonym` or `unaccent` chain.
- [Text Search Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-indexes.html)
  — GIN versus GiST for tsvector, and the expression-matching rule.

## How it works underneath

A `tsvector` is stored as a sorted array of lexemes, each followed by its
position list. Sorting is what makes `@@` cheap: matching a query term
against a vector is a binary search, and matching a conjunction is a series
of them. Deduplication happens at construction, and positions are stored as
16-bit values with the weight packed into the top two bits, which is why
the position limit is 16383 and why there are exactly four weights.

The parser is a state machine over the input, and it recognises far more
than words: URLs, email addresses, host names, file paths, version numbers,
scientific notation, hyphenated compounds. Each type gets its own
dictionary chain, which is how a configuration can stem English words while
leaving URLs alone. `ts_debug('english', 'text')` shows you the whole
pipeline per token, and it is the tool to reach for when a search does not
match what you expected — it tells you the token type, the dictionaries
tried, and the lexemes produced.

GIN over a tsvector stores each lexeme as a key with a posting list of
row pointers. A conjunctive query intersects posting lists; a disjunctive
query unions them. Because a GIN entry is a lexeme and not a document, the
index is naturally shared across the whole corpus and its size grows with
the vocabulary rather than with the corpus length. `ts_rank` cannot be
answered from the index at all — the index says which rows match, and
ranking then reads those rows' vectors from the heap.

GiST also indexes tsvector, using a signature (a bloom filter of the
lexemes) rather than the lexemes themselves. That makes it much smaller and
lossy: it produces false positives that must be rechecked against the heap.
GiST is the right choice when the index must be updated constantly and
search latency matters less; GIN is right for read-mostly corpora, which is
almost all of them.

## Historical context

Text search began as `tsearch2`, a contrib module, and was merged into core
in 8.3 — which is when `tsvector`, `tsquery`, `@@` and the configuration
machinery became built-ins. `websearch_to_tsquery` is much newer, arriving
in 11, and its absence for a decade is why so much existing code passes
user input to `plainto_tsquery` and loses phrase support. Stored generated
columns arrived in 12, replacing the older pattern of a trigger maintaining
a `tsvector` column, which you will still meet in older schemas and which
is worth recognising: a `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE` trigger calling
`tsvector_update_trigger`.

## Performance notes

The dominant cost in a search page is usually not matching. It is ranking
and highlighting. Matching is an index lookup; ranking reads every matched
row's vector; highlighting re-parses every returned row's original text.
For a query matching a hundred rows, all three are trivial. For a query
matching two hundred thousand — a common word, a single-letter search, a
user who typed nothing — ranking dominates and no index helps, because the
work is proportional to matches, not to the corpus.

The mitigations, in the order you should apply them: reject or expand
queries that are too broad before running them; use a stored generated
column so ranking reads a column rather than recomputing a vector; apply
`ts_headline` in an outer query after `LIMIT`; and if ranking still
dominates, consider `ts_rank_cd` on a smaller candidate set produced by a
stricter query, rather than ranking everything.

Index build and maintenance also deserve a number. GIN over a million
review bodies takes on the order of a minute to build and is a substantial
fraction of the table's size. Its `fastupdate` mechanism buffers inserts in
a pending list, which keeps writes cheap and makes the first query after a
bulk load pay the merge cost. On a write-heavy corpus, either tune
`gin_pending_list_limit` or turn `fastupdate` off and accept slower writes
for predictable reads.

## When not to use it

PostgreSQL full-text search is excellent for searching your own data with
your own rules, in one language, at a scale where a single machine's index
fits comfortably. It is not a search engine, and the honest boundaries are
worth knowing before someone promises otherwise.

It does not do typo tolerance. `battrey` matches nothing, ever, because the
stemmer is not a spell checker. That is the next sector's job, and the two
are usually combined: full-text for the words, trigram for the typos.

It does not do relevance learning, per-user ranking signals, or anything
that requires feedback loops. `ts_rank` is a fixed formula over term
frequency and weights.

It does not do faceted search or aggregation over a scored result set
efficiently at large scale — you can write it, but you will be ranking
everything to count anything.

And it does not do multilingual well without design work. One configuration
per index expression means one language per index, so a genuinely
multilingual corpus needs a language column, per-language partial indexes
or a per-row configuration, and a query layer that knows which to use. That
is all buildable, and it is the point at which some teams reasonably decide
to run a dedicated search service instead — with the sober understanding
that they now have two datastores to keep in sync, which is a cost paid
forever in exchange for capability they may not need.

## Exercise 1 — what the dictionary did

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Watch the `english` configuration take a sentence
apart.

Return one row with four columns, in this order, all computed from the
literal `'The batteries were excellent, and the running lights lasted.'`:

- `vec` — the `tsvector` produced by `to_tsvector` with the `english`
  configuration
- `n_lexemes` — how many lexemes are in it
- `has_battery` — boolean: does `vec` match the query `battery`
- `has_the` — boolean: does `vec` match the query `the`

Both booleans use `plainto_tsquery('english', ...)` on the right-hand side.

`has_battery` is **true** even though the word in the text is `batteries`,
because both stem to the same lexeme. `has_the` is **false** even though
the word `the` is right there, because it is a stopword and never became a
lexeme at all.

```
uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex1
```

## Hint 1

Three functions: one builds the vector, one measures it, one builds a
query. The match operator between a vector and a query is two characters.

## Hint 2

The measuring function is the general-purpose one, applied to a tsvector:

```sql
SELECT length(to_tsvector('english', 'a quick brown fox'));
```

## Hint 3

Write the vector expression once in a subquery or CTE and refer to it three
times — repeating a `to_tsvector` call four times in one row is exactly the
habit this course is trying to break, even where it costs nothing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it by predicting the output first. Write down which of the ten
words you expect to survive, and what each survivor will look like. Then
run it. The two words most people get wrong are `lights` (survives,
stemmed) and `and` (dropped).

## Hint 2

If a result surprises you, `ts_debug` explains it token by token: run
`SELECT * FROM ts_debug('english', 'The batteries were excellent.');` in
the lab and read the `dictionaries` and `lexemes` columns. That function is
the single most useful debugging tool in this sector.

## Hint 3

One detail to notice in the vector's printed form: the numbers after each
lexeme are positions in the *original token stream*, not in the lexeme
list. `excel` sitting at position 4 tells you three tokens preceded it,
including the ones that were dropped. That is how phrase search can still
work after stopword removal.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex1 — what the dictionary did
WITH d(vec) AS (
  SELECT to_tsvector('english',
           'The batteries were excellent, and the running lights lasted.')
)
SELECT vec,
       length(vec)                                     AS n_lexemes,
       vec @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery')    AS has_battery,
       vec @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'the')        AS has_the
FROM d;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex1 — lexemes counted by unnesting the vector
SELECT to_tsvector('english',
         'The batteries were excellent, and the running lights lasted.') AS vec,
       (SELECT count(*)::int
        FROM unnest(to_tsvector('english',
               'The batteries were excellent, and the running lights lasted.'))
       ) AS n_lexemes,
       to_tsvector('english',
         'The batteries were excellent, and the running lights lasted.')
         @@ to_tsquery('english', 'battery') AS has_battery,
       to_tsvector('english',
         'The batteries were excellent, and the running lights lasted.')
         @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'the') AS has_the;
