exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the failure this exercise is preventing. `to_tsquery` parses its
input as an operator expression, so a stray quote, a bare hyphen, an
unbalanced parenthesis or the word `and` on its own raises
`syntax error in tsquery`. If that function is reachable from a text input
field, your search endpoint has a trivially reachable 500 — and, in older
code that builds the query string by concatenation, worse.

## Hint 2

Now look at what each builder does with the *meaning*. `plainto_tsquery`
ANDs every surviving word, so quotes and the minus sign are discarded: the
user's negation is ignored and they get results they explicitly excluded.
`phraseto_tsquery` treats the whole input as one phrase, which is wrong for
a query with a negation in it. Only `websearch_to_tsquery` honours the
syntax the user actually typed.

## Hint 3

Worth running in the lab: feed all four builders the string `battery &&&
life` and compare. Three return something sensible; one raises. That is the
whole decision, and it takes ten seconds to make it permanent.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex2 — four ways to ask
WITH d(vec) AS (
  SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The battery life is dead short.')
), q AS (
  SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')      AS plain_q,
         phraseto_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')     AS phrase_q,
         websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead') AS web_q
)
SELECT q.plain_q::text,
       q.phrase_q::text,
       q.web_q::text,
       d.vec @@ q.plain_q  AS plain_match,
       d.vec @@ q.phrase_q AS phrase_match,
       d.vec @@ q.web_q    AS web_match
FROM d, q;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex2 — builders inlined, document built twice
SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')::text      AS plain_q,
       phraseto_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')::text     AS phrase_q,
       websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')::text AS web_q,
       to_tsvector('english', 'The battery life is dead short.')
         @@ plainto_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')       AS plain_match,
       to_tsvector('english', 'The battery life is dead short.')
         @@ phraseto_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')      AS phrase_match,
       to_tsvector('english', 'The battery life is dead short.')
         @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', '"battery life" -dead')  AS web_match;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — search the corpus

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Search the million review bodies the way a
production endpoint would.

Return the ten matching reviews with the **lowest ids** for the user query
`durable battery -broken`: two columns, `id` and `product_id`, **ordered by
`id` ascending, limited to 10**.

Use `websearch_to_tsquery` with the `english` configuration against
`to_tsvector('english', body)`. Spell the vector expression exactly as
lesson 41's index spells it — if you write anything else, the query is
correct and the plan is a sequential scan over a million rows.

```
uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One predicate, one ordering, one limit. The predicate is the match
operator between a vector built from `body` and a query built from the
user's string.

## Hint 2

The shape, with a different query builder:

```sql
SELECT id FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'durable')
ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;
```

## Hint 3

Swap the builder for the web-search one and pass the user string
unmodified, negation and all. Do not strip the leading hyphen or quote
anything — the builder's job is to interpret that, and pre-processing it
yourself is how search boxes acquire mysterious behaviour.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the plan. Run your query under `EXPLAIN` and look for
`Bitmap Index Scan` on the GIN index. If you see `Seq Scan` with a filter,
the expression in your `WHERE` clause is not the expression the index was
built on — check the configuration name first, then the exact function.

## Hint 2

Then look at where the `ORDER BY id LIMIT 10` is evaluated. The index finds
the matches; the sort happens afterwards, over all of them. That is fine
for a selective query and terrible for a broad one, which is why real
search endpoints order by rank with a bounded limit rather than by id over
an unbounded match set.

## Hint 3

Try the same query with the negation removed and compare the match counts
with `count(*)`. The `-broken` term costs the index nothing — negation is
applied as a filter on the candidate rows, not as an index lookup — which
is worth knowing before you build a UI that encourages long strings of
exclusions.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex3 — search the corpus
SELECT id, product_id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body)
      @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'durable battery -broken')
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex3 — the query built explicitly with operators
SELECT id, product_id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body)
      @@ to_tsquery('english', 'durable & battery & !broken')
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — rank, and normalise

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Rank the same matches two different ways and show
that the order is not the same.

For reviews matching `plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery')`, take the
**twenty lowest ids** as your candidate set, and return five columns for
each of them:

- `id`
- `len` — the number of lexemes in the review's vector
- `rank_raw` — `ts_rank` with no normalisation flag
- `rank_norm` — `ts_rank` with normalisation `32|2` (bounded, and divided
  by document length)
- `rank_rank` — the position of this row when ordered by `rank_raw`
  descending then `id` ascending, as an integer starting at 1

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Look down the `len` and `rank_raw` columns together: without
normalisation, longer documents score higher for the same term, because
the raw score counts occurrences. Bit 2 divides that back out.

```
uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Pick the candidate set first in a CTE — matching reviews, ordered by id,
limited to twenty — then compute the four derived columns over it.

## Hint 2

`ts_rank` takes the vector and the query, and optionally a normalisation
integer as the last argument:

```sql
SELECT ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body),
               plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery'), 2)
FROM reviews WHERE id = 1;
```

## Hint 3

For `rank_rank`, this is a window function over the candidate set, ordered
the way the prompt says. Combining a bitmask is just the `|` operator on
two integers — write `32|2` and PostgreSQL will do the arithmetic, or write
the sum yourself if you prefer to see the number.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what `ts_rank` is measuring. It is a function of how many times
each query lexeme occurs and what weight each occurrence carries — nothing
else. Not document quality, not recency, not popularity, not how close the
terms are. A review that says "battery" eight times ranks above one that
says it twice and answers the question.

## Hint 2

That is why normalisation exists, and why choosing a bit is a product
decision rather than a technical one. Dividing by length says "a short
document that mentions the term is at least as relevant as a long one".
Dividing by unique word count says something subtly different. Bit 32 does
not change the order at all — it only rescales into 0..1 so that scores
from different queries can be compared or blended with other signals.

## Hint 3

The production shape you are building toward: rank in the database, then
blend with your own signals — recency, rating, sales — in one arithmetic
expression, ordering by the blend. That only works if the text score is
bounded, which is the argument for bit 32 that no documentation makes
loudly enough.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex4 — rank, and normalise
WITH q AS (SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery') AS q),
candidates AS (
  SELECT r.id, to_tsvector('english', r.body) AS vec
  FROM reviews r, q
  WHERE to_tsvector('english', r.body) @@ q.q
  ORDER BY r.id
  LIMIT 20
)
SELECT c.id,
       length(c.vec)                        AS len,
       ts_rank(c.vec, q.q)                  AS rank_raw,
       ts_rank(c.vec, q.q, 32|2)            AS rank_norm,
       (row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank(c.vec, q.q) DESC, c.id))::int
                                            AS rank_rank
FROM candidates c, q
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex4 — vectors recomputed, ranking via a rank() window
WITH candidates AS (
  SELECT id, body
  FROM reviews
  WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery')
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 20
), scored AS (
  SELECT id,
         length(to_tsvector('english', body)) AS len,
         ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body),
                 plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery')) AS rank_raw,
         ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body),
                 plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery'), 34) AS rank_norm
  FROM candidates
)
SELECT id, len, rank_raw, rank_norm,
       (row_number() OVER (ORDER BY rank_raw DESC, id))::int AS rank_rank
FROM scored
ORDER BY id;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — weights

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. A product's name should count for more than its
description.

For the products with `id <= 100`, build a weighted vector — the `name`
weighted `A`, the `description` weighted `B` — and rank them against
`plainto_tsquery('english', 'garden')`.

Return four columns in this order:

- `id`
- `name`
- `rank_default` — `ts_rank` with the default weights
- `rank_name_only` — `ts_rank` with the weight array
  `'{0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0}'`, which scores A-weighted matches and ignores
  everything else

Keep only rows whose weighted vector matches the query, and order by
`rank_default` **descending**, then `id` ascending.

The second weight array is the interesting one: it is `{D, C, B, A}`, so
that array means "only the name matters". Products matching only in the
description will score 0 there.

```
uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two vectors, each `setweight`-ed, then concatenated with `||`. The result
is one vector in which every lexeme remembers which field it came from.

## Hint 2

The construction:

```sql
SELECT setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'a title'), 'A')
    || setweight(to_tsvector('english', 'some body text'), 'D');
```

## Hint 3

`ts_rank`'s optional first argument is the weight array. Build the combined
vector once in a CTE, then call `ts_rank` twice against it with different
first arguments. Watch out for NULL descriptions if any exist —
concatenating a NULL vector produces NULL, and `coalesce` on the text
before vectorising is the usual guard.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reversal is the whole trap. `ts_rank`'s array is `{D, C, B, A}` —
lowest weight first — while `setweight` labels run A (most important) to D.
Anybody writing the array in the order they think about weights gets a
ranking that is precisely upside down and looks, at a glance, plausible.

## Hint 2

The second trap is the default. If you never call `setweight`, every lexeme
is weight D, and D's default multiplier is 0.1. That does not change the
*order* of a single-field ranking, since everything is scaled equally, but
it does mean raw scores from a weighted and an unweighted corpus are not
comparable — another reason to normalise with bit 32 before blending
scores with anything else.

## Hint 3

Design-wise, this is where a stored generated column earns its keep. A
weighted vector built from two columns is an expression you do not want
written out in five different queries, each with its own chance of a
transposed letter. Compute it once in the table definition, index that, and
let every query say `tsv @@ query`. The challenge builds exactly that.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex5 — weights
WITH v AS (
  SELECT id, name,
         setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(name, '')), 'A')
      || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(description, '')), 'B')
           AS vec
  FROM products
  WHERE id <= 100
), q AS (SELECT plainto_tsquery('english', 'garden') AS q)
SELECT v.id,
       v.name,
       ts_rank(v.vec, q.q)                                AS rank_default,
       ts_rank('{0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0}'::float4[], v.vec, q.q) AS rank_name_only
FROM v, q
WHERE v.vec @@ q.q
ORDER BY rank_default DESC, v.id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex5 — weighted vector assembled in a lateral
SELECT p.id,
       p.name,
       ts_rank(w.vec, plainto_tsquery('english', 'garden')) AS rank_default,
       ts_rank(ARRAY[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]::float4[], w.vec,
               plainto_tsquery('english', 'garden'))        AS rank_name_only
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(p.name, '')), 'A')
      || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(p.description, '')), 'B')
         AS vec
) w
WHERE p.id <= 100
  AND w.vec @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'garden')
ORDER BY rank_default DESC, p.id;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — phrases and distance

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Phrase search is position arithmetic, and the
distance is adjustable.

Return one row with five columns, in this order, all evaluated against the
document `'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.'`
vectorised with the `english` configuration:

- `adjacent` — does it match `phraseto_tsquery('english', 'red wine')`
- `explicit_adjacent` — does it match `to_tsquery('english', 'red <-> wine')`
- `within_two` — does it match `to_tsquery('english', 'red <2> wine')`
- `within_three` — does it match `to_tsquery('english', 'red <3> wine')`
- `plain_and` — does it match `plainto_tsquery('english', 'red wine')`

`red wine` appears adjacently in the second half of the sentence, so the
first three are all true. Work out what `<2>` and `<3>` mean before you
run it — the number is the distance between the two lexemes' positions, and
`<->` is exactly `<1>`.

```
uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Five match tests against one vector. Build the vector once and reuse it.

## Hint 2

The distance operator lives inside a tsquery, and `to_tsquery` is the
builder that accepts it:

```sql
SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'quick <2> fox')::text;
```

## Hint 3

Nothing here needs a table. A `WITH` clause holding the vector, then a
single `SELECT` with five boolean expressions. The only thinking required
is predicting each answer first — and if `within_two` surprises you,
remember that stopwords still occupy positions.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with the positions. Vectorise the document on its own and read the
numbers: `'red':2,10` and `'wine':4,11` or similar. Phrase matching asks
whether there is a pair of positions with exactly the required difference —
so `red <1> wine` is satisfied by the pair at 10 and 11, and `red <2> wine`
by the pair at 2 and 4.

## Hint 2

That is why `<N>` is "at distance exactly N", not "within N". A query for
`red <3> wine` fails on a document where they are adjacent, which surprises
people who read it as a proximity search. If you want "within N", you write
the disjunction of the distances, or you use `ts_rank_cd`, which scores by
proximity rather than filtering on it.

## Hint 3

Stopword positions are the second surprise. `the` is dropped from the
vector but its position is still consumed, so `red <2> wine` in "red *the*
wine" would match while the lexemes are adjacent in the vector. Positions
are of tokens, not of lexemes, and that is deliberate: it keeps phrase
search honest about the original text.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex6 — phrases and distance
WITH d(vec) AS (
  SELECT to_tsvector('english',
           'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.')
)
SELECT vec @@ phraseto_tsquery('english', 'red wine')   AS adjacent,
       vec @@ to_tsquery('english', 'red <-> wine')     AS explicit_adjacent,
       vec @@ to_tsquery('english', 'red <2> wine')     AS within_two,
       vec @@ to_tsquery('english', 'red <3> wine')     AS within_three,
       vec @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'red wine')    AS plain_and
FROM d;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex6 — same tests, queries built by casting text
SELECT to_tsvector('english',
         'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.')
         @@ phraseto_tsquery('english', 'red wine')          AS adjacent,
       to_tsvector('english',
         'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.')
         @@ ('red <-> wine')::tsquery                        AS explicit_adjacent,
       to_tsvector('english',
         'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.')
         @@ ('red <2> wine')::tsquery                        AS within_two,
       to_tsvector('english',
         'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.')
         @@ ('red <3> wine')::tsquery                        AS within_three,
       to_tsvector('english',
         'The red table wine was excellent with the red wine sauce.')
         @@ ('red & wine')::tsquery                          AS plain_and;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — two configurations

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Compare `simple` and `english` on the same three
strings.

Work from this exact input, inline:

```sql
(VALUES (1, 'The running batteries were excellent'),
        (2, 'SKU-4242 model XR-9'),
        (3, 'A the of and')) AS t(id, txt)
```

Return six columns in this order, ordered by `id` ascending (3 rows):

- `id`
- `simple_vec` — `to_tsvector('simple', txt)`
- `english_vec` — `to_tsvector('english', txt)`
- `simple_n` — lexeme count of the first
- `english_n` — lexeme count of the second
- `english_finds_batteries` — does `english_vec` match
  `plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery')`

Row 3 is the one that makes the point: `simple_n` is 4 and `english_n` is
**0**, because every word in it is an English stopword. A document can
vectorise to nothing, and a document that vectorises to nothing can never
match any query.

```
uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The only difference between the two vector columns is the first argument.
Everything else — the counting function, the match operator — you have
already used.

## Hint 2

An empty vector prints as an empty string and has a length of zero:

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'the and of'), length(to_tsvector('english', 'the and of'));
```

## Hint 3

Six columns over a three-row `VALUES` list. The decision left to you is
which configuration to use in the final boolean — the column is named for
the vector it tests, and the query builder's configuration should match the
vector's, or you are comparing lexemes produced by two different stemmers.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Look hard at row 2. `SKU-4242` and `XR-9` are not English words, and the
`english` configuration will still run them through the parser's
hyphenated-word rules, producing lexemes for the parts as well as the
whole. Whether that helps or hurts depends entirely on whether users search
for `4242` or for `SKU-4242`, and you cannot have both behaviours from one
configuration.

## Hint 2

Which is the argument for indexing identifiers with `simple` and prose with
`english`, in two separate expressions, and searching both. That is a real
pattern: a product search that matches SKUs exactly and descriptions
loosely is two indexes and an `OR`, not one clever configuration.

## Hint 3

Row 3 has a production consequence worth stating plainly: a short document
made entirely of stopwords is invisible to English full-text search
forever. If your corpus contains such rows — one-word reviews, titles like
"The One" — either search them with `simple` too, or accept that they
cannot be found by text at all and give the user another route to them.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex7 — two configurations
SELECT id,
       to_tsvector('simple', txt)          AS simple_vec,
       to_tsvector('english', txt)         AS english_vec,
       length(to_tsvector('simple', txt))  AS simple_n,
       length(to_tsvector('english', txt)) AS english_n,
       to_tsvector('english', txt) @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery')
         AS english_finds_batteries
FROM (VALUES (1, 'The running batteries were excellent'),
             (2, 'SKU-4242 model XR-9'),
             (3, 'A the of and')) AS t(id, txt)
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / ex7 — vectors computed once per row in a lateral
SELECT t.id,
       v.simple_vec,
       v.english_vec,
       coalesce((SELECT count(*)::int FROM unnest(v.simple_vec)), 0)  AS simple_n,
       coalesce((SELECT count(*)::int FROM unnest(v.english_vec)), 0) AS english_n,
       v.english_vec @@ to_tsquery('english', 'battery')
         AS english_finds_batteries
FROM (VALUES (1, 'The running batteries were excellent'),
             (2, 'SKU-4242 model XR-9'),
             (3, 'A the of and')) AS t(id, txt)
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT to_tsvector('simple', t.txt)  AS simple_vec,
         to_tsvector('english', t.txt) AS english_vec
) v
ORDER BY t.id;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt: ## Exercise 8 — the snippet Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Produce the result list a search page renders: matches, ranked, with a highlighted extract of each. For reviews matching `websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery life')`, return the top five by rank, with three columns in this order: - `id` - `rank` — `ts_rank` with normalisation 32 - `snippet` — `ts_headline` over the review `body`, with the options string `'StartSel=, StopSel=, MaxWords=18, MinWords=5'` **Ordered by `rank` descending, then `id` ascending, limited to 5.** The structural requirement: `ts_headline` must be applied **after** the limit, not before. Do the matching, ranking and limiting in a subquery, and decorate only the five rows that survive. A plan that highlights every matching review and then throws almost all of them away is the single most common performance bug on a search page. ``` uv run dojo test v3c04_fulltext ex8 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two levels. The inner query finds, ranks and limits. The outer query adds
the expensive column to whatever the inner one returned.

## Hint 2

`ts_headline` takes a configuration, the original document text, the query,
and an options string:

```sql
SELECT ts_headline('english', body, plainto_tsquery('english', 'battery'),
                   'MaxWords=10, MinWords=3')
FROM reviews WHERE id = 1;
```

Note it takes the *text*, not the vector — it has to re-parse the original
to find the words in context.

## Hint 3

Carry `body` through the inner query so the outer one can decorate it, and
drop it from the final select list. The query builder appears in three
places — the filter, the rank and the headline — so put it in a CTE or
repeat it carefully; a mismatch between the three is a snippet that
highlights nothing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reason about the cost model. Matching is an index lookup. Ranking reads the
matched rows. Headlining re-parses the full original text of every row it
touches, with no index involvement whatsoever, and the text of a review is
much larger than its vector. So the cost of a search page is roughly
`(matches × rank) + (headlined rows × parse)`, and only the second factor is
under your control.

## Hint 2

Which means the ordering of operations in your query is a performance
decision, not a style one. `SELECT ts_headline(...) FROM reviews WHERE ...
ORDER BY rank LIMIT 5` computes the headline for every matching row, then
sorts, then discards all but five. Wrapping the limit in a subquery reduces
that to exactly five parses.

## Hint 3

Confirm it rather than believing it: run both spellings under `EXPLAIN
(ANALYZE, TIMING OFF)` in the lab against a broad query term and compare
the total times. The difference on a term matching tens of thousands of
reviews is not subtle, and it is the kind of evidence that ends an
architecture argument in one screenshot.

references.solution.sql: -- v3c04_fulltext / ex8 — the snippet WITH q AS (SELECT websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery life') AS q), top5 AS ( SELECT r.id, r.body, ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', r.body), q.q, 32) AS rank FROM reviews r, q WHERE to_tsvector('english', r.body) @@ q.q ORDER BY rank DESC, r.id LIMIT 5 ) SELECT t.id, t.rank, ts_headline('english', t.body, q.q, 'StartSel=, StopSel=, MaxWords=18, MinWords=5') AS snippet FROM top5 t, q ORDER BY t.rank DESC, t.id;
references.expected.sql: -- v3c04_fulltext / ex8 — the same two-stage shape with a plain subquery SELECT id, rank, ts_headline('english', body, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery life'), 'StartSel=, StopSel=, MaxWords=18, MinWords=5') AS snippet FROM ( SELECT id, body, ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body), websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery life'), 32) AS rank FROM reviews WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'battery life') ORDER BY rank DESC, id LIMIT 5 ) s ORDER BY rank DESC, id;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a searchable table

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Build a small searchable table the way you
would build a real one, and prove it works.

Write a script that:

1. Creates a table `docs` with `id int primary key`, `title text not null`,
   `body text not null`, and a **stored generated column** `tsv tsvector`
   holding `setweight(to_tsvector('english', title), 'A')` concatenated
   with `setweight(to_tsvector('english', body), 'B')`.
2. Creates a GIN index on `tsv`.
3. Inserts these four rows (id, title, body):
   - `1, 'Battery life', 'The cordless drill runs for hours.'`
   - `2, 'Cordless drill review', 'Battery drains quickly under load.'`
   - `3, 'Garden hose', 'Kinks near the tap but the fittings are solid.'`
   - `4, 'Drill bits', 'A set of bits for wood and masonry.'`
4. Finishes with a query that searches for `websearch_to_tsquery('english',
   'drill battery')` and returns four columns — `id`, `title`, `rank`
   (`ts_rank` over `tsv` with normalisation 32) and `snippet`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A generated column is declared inline in `CREATE TABLE` with `GENERATED
ALWAYS AS (<expression>) STORED`. The expression must be immutable, which
is why the configuration name has to be written out.

## Hint 2

The declaration looks like this:

```sql
tsv tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED
```

Your version concatenates two `setweight` calls instead of that single
call.

## Hint 3

Two details decide whether it compiles. The generated expression may
reference other columns of the same row but nothing outside it — no
subqueries, no other tables. And `coalesce` is worth wrapping around both
text columns even though both are `NOT NULL` here, because the day one
becomes nullable, a NULL vector concatenation silently empties the whole
column.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand what the generated column buys before you write it. The index
expression and the query expression can no longer disagree, because there
is only one expression and it lives in the table definition. Every drift
bug from this sector's "common mistakes" list is structurally impossible
once the vector is a column.

## Hint 2

Understand the cost too. The vector is stored, so the table grows —
typically by a good fraction of the text's size — and every insert and
update to `title` or `body` recomputes it. That is the same work the
expression index would have done, moved from index build time to row write
time, plus the storage. On a read-heavy corpus this is an obviously good
trade; on a write-heavy one, measure.

## Hint 3

One more thing worth knowing about generated columns: you cannot insert
into them, and `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET EXPRESSION` (16 and
later) rewrites the table when you change the definition. So changing the
weighting scheme later is a table rewrite, which is an argument for getting
the weights right early — or for keeping the expression index approach on
very large tables, where a `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on a new expression
is the gentler migration.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3c04_fulltext / challenge — a searchable table
CREATE TABLE docs (
  id    int  PRIMARY KEY,
  title text NOT NULL,
  body  text NOT NULL,
  tsv   tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
          setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title, '')), 'A')
       || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body,  '')), 'B')
        ) STORED
);

CREATE INDEX docs_tsv_idx ON docs USING gin (tsv);

INSERT INTO docs (id, title, body) VALUES
  (1, 'Battery life',          'The cordless drill runs for hours.'),
  (2, 'Cordless drill review', 'Battery drains quickly under load.'),
  (3, 'Garden hose',           'Kinks near the tap but the fittings are solid.'),
  (4, 'Drill bits',            'A set of bits for wood and masonry.');

SELECT d.id,
       d.title,
       ts_rank(d.tsv, websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'drill battery'), 32)
         AS rank,
       ts_headline('english', d.body,
                   websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'drill battery'),
                   'MaxWords=12, MinWords=3') AS snippet
FROM docs d
WHERE d.tsv @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'drill battery')
ORDER BY rank DESC, d.id;

FROM hits h, q


when the expression is not a bare function call — here it is one, so a
single pair suffices.

## Hint 3

The final query's `WHERE` clause is a match between the same vector

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The rejection has a precise reason worth being able to state. An index
stores precomputed values, so the expression producing them must be
`IMMUTABLE`: same input, same output, forever. `to_tsvector(text)` reads
`default_text_search_config`, a session GUC, so the same input can produce
different output in two sessions. It is marked `STABLE`, and PostgreSQL
refuses to build an index on a `STABLE` expression.

## Hint 2

Now consider the failure mode that rule prevents. Suppose it were allowed:
a session with the setting on `english` inserts a row and stores stemmed
lexemes; a session on `simple` inserts another and stores unstemmed ones.
The index now contains entries that disagree about what the words mean, and
queries return wrong answers with no error anywhere. Immutability is not
pedantry; it is the guarantee the index is built on.

## Hint 3

The same rule explains a family of related refusals: you cannot index
`now()`, or a `timestamptz`-to-`text` cast that depends on `TimeZone`, or a
`lower()` call under a non-deterministic collation in some configurations.
Whenever `CREATE INDEX` complains that a function must be immutable, the
question to ask is "what setting could change this result", and the answer
is always there.

lessons.title: V3·C5 — Trigram and fuzzy matching
lessons.summary: Full-text search cannot find a misspelling, and LIKE '%son%' cannot use a B-tree. Trigrams solve both problems with one idea: chop strings into three-character pieces and index the pieces. This sector covers similarity, the threshold, word similarity, KNN distance ordering, and where Levenshtein still beats all of it.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·C5 — Trigram and fuzzy matching

The previous sector's search is exact about words. Type `battrey` into it
and you get nothing — the stemmer is not a spell checker, and a lexeme that
does not exist in the corpus matches no posting list. Meanwhile lesson 33
left a different debt: `WHERE name LIKE '%son%'` cannot use a B-tree,
because a B-tree descends on a prefix and there is no prefix. Both problems
have one answer, and it is a good one.

Chop every string into overlapping three-character pieces. `hello` becomes
the set `{"  h", " he", hel, ell, llo, "lo "}` — note the padding, which is
what makes prefixes and suffixes matter. Now two strings can be compared by
how much of their trigram sets they share, and — the part that pays — the
trigrams can go in a GIN or GiST index, so `LIKE '%son%'` becomes a lookup
of the trigrams `son`, `%so`, `on%` rather than a scan.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;

SELECT show_trgm('hello');
-- {"  h"," he",ell,hel,llo,"lo "}

SELECT similarity('hello', 'helo');      -- shared trigrams / union: ~0.57
SELECT 'hello' % 'helo';                 -- true, if similarity >= threshold
SELECT 'hello' <-> 'helo';               -- the distance: 1 - similarity
```

`similarity(a, b)` is the count of shared trigrams over the count of
trigrams in the union — a number in 0..1 that says how alike two strings
are, character by character, with no notion of words or meaning.

The `%` operator is `similarity(a, b) >= pg_trgm.similarity_threshold`,
which defaults to `0.3`:

```sql
SET pg_trgm.similarity_threshold = 0.5;   -- or SELECT set_limit(0.5)
```

That setting is the single most consequential knob in this sector. Too low
and every search returns half the table; too high and typos stop matching.
It is per-session, which means it belongs in your application's connection
setup, not in a comment somebody forgot.

When the two strings are very different in length — a search term against a
whole sentence — plain `similarity` is useless, because the long string's
trigram count swamps the shared ones. That is what word similarity is for:

```sql
similarity('drill', 'a cordless drill for wood')          -- ~0.19, poor
word_similarity('drill', 'a cordless drill for wood')     -- 1.0
strict_word_similarity('drill', 'a cordless drill kit')   -- 1.0
```

`word_similarity(a, b)` finds the extent of `b` that best matches `a`;
`strict_word_similarity` requires that extent to align with word
boundaries. Their operators are `<%` and `<<%`, and note the direction:
the short pattern goes on the left.

Two index families, and the difference matters:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin  (name gin_trgm_ops);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING gist (name gist_trgm_ops);
```

GIN is faster and larger and answers `LIKE`, `ILIKE`, `~`, `~*`, `%` and
`<%`. GiST answers all of those **and** supports distance ordering:
`ORDER BY name <-> 'sarah' LIMIT 5` becomes a K-nearest-neighbour index
scan instead of a sort over the whole table. If you need "the ten closest
names", you need GiST.

Finally, a different toolbox for a different question:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS fuzzystrmatch;
SELECT levenshtein('bakery', 'bakers');   -- 1, edit distance
SELECT soundex('Robert'), soundex('Rupert');       -- both R163
SELECT metaphone('Thompson', 8), difference('Robert', 'Rupert');
```

Levenshtein counts edits; trigram similarity counts shared pieces. The two
disagree in useful ways: a single transposition (`Johnson` to `Jonhson`)
barely dents trigram similarity and costs two Levenshtein edits, while a
short word inside a long one scores badly on trigrams and well on nothing
at all. Neither is a superset of the other, and the standard production
arrangement uses both — trigrams to produce candidates from an index,
Levenshtein to rank the handful that survive, because edit distance has no
index and never will.

They Soundex and metaphone encode *pronunciation*, which
catches `Smith`/`Smyth` where trigrams do less well and misses everything
in a language they were not designed for — which is English, specifically
American English, specifically surnames.

One more decision belongs in this briefing, because it is the one people
get wrong first: trigrams are for *short* strings. Names, titles, SKUs,
addresses, email addresses, tags. Running `%` over a million review bodies
is slow to build, enormous on disk, and imprecise — the previous sector's
full-text machinery is what prose wants. The two are complementary rather
than competing, and the last two missions here make you wire them together
in that order: words first, characters as the fallback.

## Exercise 1 — the trigrams themselves

`show_trgm`, the padding, and similarity computed by hand from the two
sets.

## Exercise 2 — the threshold is a decision

The `%` operator at two different thresholds over the same pair of strings.

## Exercise 3 — fuzzy name search

Find customers whose names are closest to a misspelling, ranked by
similarity.

## Exercise 4 — word similarity

Three similarity functions on the same short-against-long pair, and the
one that makes autocomplete work.

## Exercise 5 — distance ordering

Build a GiST trigram index and use `<->` in `ORDER BY` for a real
K-nearest-neighbour scan.

## Exercise 6 — rescuing LIKE

A GIN trigram index over the product names, and the unanchored `ILIKE`
query that finally uses an index.

## Exercise 7 — edit distance and sound

`levenshtein`, `soundex`, `metaphone` and `difference` side by side, on
pairs chosen to make each one look good and bad in turn.

## Exercise 8 — candidate duplicates

The entity-resolution query: find pairs of customer names similar enough to
be the same person, without comparing every name to every other name.

## Challenge — did you mean

Full-text search with a trigram fallback: exact word matching first, and
when that finds nothing, the closest strings instead.

## Review 1 — pick the index

Two trigram indexes on one table, three queries, and a written answer about
which index serves which — because choosing wrong here costs you either the
KNN ordering or a great deal of disk.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - v3c05_trigram_fuzzy

Trigram matching is the crudest idea in this volume and one of the most
useful. It knows nothing about language, meaning, stemming or word
boundaries. It compares strings as bags of three-character pieces, and that
turns out to be exactly the right level of ignorance for typos, name
matching and unanchored substring search.

## Notes

**Padding is why prefixes matter.** `show_trgm('cat')` returns `{"  c",
" ca", cat, "at "}` — two leading spaces before the first character, one
trailing. A string of length n yields n+1 trigrams. That padding means
`cat` and `scat` share fewer trigrams than their letters suggest, which is
usually what you want for names.

**`similarity` is symmetric and length-sensitive.** It divides shared
trigrams by the size of the union, so comparing a five-character term to a
fifty-character sentence gives a small number even when the term appears
verbatim. That is not a bug; it is the definition, and it is why word
similarity exists.

**`word_similarity(a, b)` is asymmetric.** It looks for the extent of `b`
whose trigrams best match all of `a`'s — so `word_similarity('drill',
'cordless drill')` is 1.0 while `word_similarity('cordless drill',
'drill')` is much lower. Put the short thing on the left. The operator
`<%` follows the same convention.

**`strict_word_similarity` adds word boundaries.** Plain word similarity
will happily match inside a word, so `word_similarity('ill', 'drill')` is
high. The strict variant requires the matched extent to start and end at
word boundaries, which is what you want for "does this sentence contain
something like this word".

**The threshold is a GUC, not an argument.** `%`, `<%` and `<<%` each read
their own setting: `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold`,
`pg_trgm.word_similarity_threshold`, `pg_trgm.strict_word_similarity_threshold`.
Changing one does not change the others. `set_limit()` and `show_limit()`
are the older function interface to the first of them.

**Distance is `1 - similarity`.** `<->` for similarity, `<<->` for word
similarity, `<<<->` for strict word similarity. Distances exist because
index access methods can order by them, and similarity cannot be ordered by
an index directly.

**Only GiST does KNN.** `ORDER BY col <-> 'x' LIMIT 10` with a
`gist_trgm_ops` index is a nearest-neighbour scan that stops after ten
rows. The same query with a GIN index sorts every row. This is the one
capability GIN does not have, and it is often the deciding factor.

**GIN is bigger and faster for filtering.** For `LIKE '%x%'`, `~*`, or `%`
predicates over a large table, `gin_trgm_ops` is normally the right choice
— the index is larger and slower to update, and the lookups are quicker.

**The three thresholds are independent.** Setting
`pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` changes what `%` does and leaves `<%` and
`<<%` exactly as they were. Each operator reads its own GUC, and a
connection pooler will happily hand you a session where somebody else set
one of them — which is why production code sets the ones it uses at
connection time rather than assuming defaults.

**A trigram index rescues unanchored patterns.** `LIKE '%son%'` extracts
the trigrams of the pattern, looks up rows containing all of them, and
rechecks the pattern on the candidates. Patterns shorter than three
characters extract nothing and fall back to a scan.

**Trigram matching is language-agnostic and meaning-blind.** It has no
dictionary, no stemmer and no stopword list, so it works identically on
Polish surnames and product codes — and it will happily rate `battery` and
`flattery` as close relatives. It cannot tell you which of two similar
strings is a real word, because it has no idea what a word is.

**Case and punctuation are handled for you.** Extraction lowercases and
treats non-alphanumeric characters as separators, so `O'Brien` and
`obrien` share most of their trigrams and `ILIKE` needs no `lower()`
wrapper to be index-assisted.

**Levenshtein is exact and unindexable.** It computes an edit distance
between two specific strings — excellent inside a small candidate set,
hopeless as a filter over a million rows, because there is no index for it.
The standard pattern is trigram index to narrow, Levenshtein to rank.

**Soundex and metaphone are English-specific.** They encode pronunciation
into a short code, catching `Smith`/`Smyth` and `Robert`/`Rupert`. They
also collide aggressively and mangle non-English names. Use them as one
signal among several, never alone.

## ex1 — the trigrams themselves

Computing similarity by hand from the two sets is the exercise; after this
the number stops being magic.

## ex2 — the threshold is a decision

Note the setting is per-session and survives until changed. That is why
production code sets it explicitly at connection time.

## ex3 — fuzzy name search

Without an index this scans, and on fifty thousand names that is fine. The
same query on fifty million is exercise 5's problem.

## ex4 — word similarity

The asymmetry is the whole point. Write the arguments in both orders and
watch the number change.

## ex5 — distance ordering

Read the plan: `Index Scan using ... Order By: (name <-> 'x')`. That line is
the KNN scan, and it is the reason GiST exists here.

## ex6 — rescuing LIKE

Compare with lesson 33's rule. A B-tree can serve `LIKE 'son%'` and nothing
else; a trigram index serves the unanchored case a B-tree cannot touch.

## ex7 — edit distance and sound

Look for the pairs where the two families disagree. Those disagreements are
the argument for combining them.

## ex8 — candidate duplicates

The pruning is the exercise. A self-join without a `%` predicate is
2.5 billion comparisons on this table.

## Further reading

- [pg_trgm](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/pgtrgm.html) — trigram
  extraction, all three similarity families, the GUCs and the operator
  classes.
- [fuzzystrmatch](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/fuzzystrmatch.html) —
  `levenshtein`, `soundex`, `metaphone`, `dmetaphone`, `difference`.
- [GiST Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gist.html) — the
  ordering-operator support that makes KNN scans possible.
- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html)
  — `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` and POSIX regexes, and which are index-assisted.
